PART 3:
THE
PRINCIPLES
OF STORY
DESIGN

第三部分：故事设计的原则

When forced to work within a strict framework the imagination is taxed to its utmost—and will produce its richest ideas. Given total freedom the work is likely to sprawl.

当被迫在严格的框架内工作时，想象力会得到最大程度的发挥——并由此产生最丰富的创意。而给予完全的自由，作品则很可能变得杂乱无章。

—T. S. E LIOT

——T·S·艾略特

#↩

7
7
THE SUBSTANCE OF STORY
故事的实质

From what material do we create the scenes that will one day walk and talk their way across the screen? What is the clay we twist and shape, keep or throw away? What is the “substance” of story?

我们用什么素材来创作那些终有一天会在银幕上行走、说话的场景？我们捏塑、保留或丢弃的黏土是什么？故事的“实质”是什么？

In all other arts the answer is self-evident. The composer has his instrument and the notes it sounds. The dancer calls her body her instrument. Sculptors chisel stone. Painters stir paint. All artists can lay hands on the raw material of their art—except the writer. For at the nucleus of a story is a “substance,” like the energy swirling in an atom, that’s never directly seen, heard, or touched, yet we know it and feel it. The stuff of story is alive but intangible.

在其他所有艺术领域，答案显而易见。作曲家有他的乐器和它发出的音符。舞者称自己的身体为乐器。雕塑家凿刻石头。画家搅拌颜料。所有艺术家都能接触到他们艺术的原材料——唯独作家例外。因为故事的核心是一种“物质”，如同原子中旋转的能量，它永远无法被直接看到、听到或触摸，但我们却能感知到它。故事的素材是鲜活的，却又无形无质。

“Intangible?” I hear you thinking. “But I have my words. Dialogue, description. I can put hands on my pages. The writer’s raw material is language.” In fact, it’s not, and the careers of many talented writers, especially those who come to screenwriting after a strong literary education, flounder because of the disastrous misunderstanding of this principle. For just as glass is a medium for light, air a medium for sound, language is only a medium, one of many, in fact, for storytelling. Something far more profound than mere words beats at the heart of a story.

“无形的？”我仿佛听到你在想。“但我有文字啊。对话，描写。我可以亲手触摸纸页。作家的原材料就是语言。” 事实上，并非如此。许多才华横溢的作家，尤其是那些接受过扎实文学教育后转行编剧的人，他们的职业生涯都因对这一原则的严重误解而受挫。正如玻璃是光的媒介，空气是声音的媒介，语言也只是一种媒介，事实上，它是众多叙事媒介之一。故事的核心，远比文字本身更为深刻的东西。

And at the opposite end of story sits another equally profound phenomenon: the audience’s reaction to this substance. When you think about it, going to the movies is bizarre. Hundreds of strangers sit in a blackened room, elbow to elbow, for two or more hours. They don’t go to the toilet or get a smoke. Instead, they stare wide-eyed at a screen, investing more uninterrupted concentration than they give to work, paying money to suffer emotions they’d do anything to avoid in life. From this perspective, a second question arises: What is the source of story energy? How does it compel such intense mental and sentient attention from the audience? How do stories work?

故事的另一端，存在着另一个同样深刻的现象：观众对这种内容的反应。仔细想想，去电影院看电影其实很奇特。数百名陌生人肩并肩地坐在漆黑的放映厅里，一坐就是两个多小时。他们不去洗手间，也不抽烟。相反，他们目不转睛地盯着屏幕，投入的专注力甚至超过了工作时间，花钱去体验那些他们在生活中极力想要避免的情绪。从这个角度来看，第二个问题随之而来：故事能量的来源是什么？它是如何调动观众如此强烈的精神和感官注意力的？故事是如何运作的？

The answers to these questions come when the artist explores the creative process subjectively. To understand the substance of story and how it performs, you need to view your work from the inside out, from the center of your character, looking out at the world through your character’s eyes, experiencing the story as if you were the living character yourself. To slip into this subjective and highly imaginative point of view, you need to look closely at this creature you intend to inhabit, a character. Or more specifically, a protagonist. For although the protagonist is a character like any other, as the central and essential role, he embodies all aspects of character in absolute terms.

这些问题的答案源于艺术家对创作过程的主观探索。要理解故事的本质及其运作方式，你需要从内而外地审视你的作品，从角色的中心出发，透过角色的眼睛观察世界，如同身临其境般体验故事。要进入这种主观且极富想象力的视角，你需要仔细审视你想要塑造的这个角色，或者更确切地说，是主角。因为尽管主角和其他角色一样，但作为核心和关键角色，他绝对地体现了角色的所有特质。

THE PROTAGONIST

主角

Generally, the protagonist is a single character. A story, however, could be driven by a duo, such as THELMA & LOUISE; a trio, THE WITCHES OF EASTWICK; more, THE SEVEN SAMURAI or THE DIRTY DOZEN. In THE BATTLESHIP POTEMKIN an entire class of people, the proletariat, create a massive Plural-Protagonist.

通常，主角是单一角色。然而，故事也可以由两人组合推动，例如《末路狂花》；三人组合，例如《东镇女巫》；更多角色，例如《七武士》或《十二金刚》。在《战舰波将金号》中，整个阶层——无产阶级——共同构成了一个庞大的多元主角。

For two or more characters to form a Plural-Protagonist, two conditions must be met: First, all individuals in the group share the same desire. Second, in the struggle to achieve this desire, they mutually suffer and benefit. If one has a success, all benefit. If one has a setback, all suffer. Within a Plural-Protagonist, motivation, action, and consequence are communal.

要使两个或多个角色构成多元主角，必须满足两个条件：首先，群体中的所有成员都拥有相同的愿望。其次，在实现这一愿望的过程中，他们彼此承受痛苦，也彼此受益。如果其中一人成功，所有人都会受益；如果其中一人遭遇挫折，所有人都会遭受损失。在多元主角中，动机、行动和后果都是共同的。

A story may, on the other hand, be Multiprotagonist. Here, unlike the Plural-Protagonist, characters pursue separate and individual desires, suffering and benefiting independently: PULP FICTION, HANNAH AND HER SISTERS, PARENTHOOD, DINER, DO THE RIGHT THING, THE BREAKFAST CLUB, EAT DRINK MAN WOMAN, PELLE THE CONQUEROR, HOPE AND GLORY, HIGH HOPES. Robert Altman is the master of this design: A WEDDING, NASHVILLE, SHORT CUTS.

另一方面，故事也可以是多主角叙事。与多元主角叙事不同，多主角叙事中的角色追求各自独立的欲望，各自承受痛苦和收获：例如《低俗小说》、《汉娜姐妹》、《为人父母》、《餐馆》、《为所应为》、《早餐俱乐部》、《饮食男女》、《征服者佩尔》、《希望与荣耀》、《远大前程》。罗伯特·奥特曼是这种叙事结构的个中高手：例如《婚礼》、《纳什维尔》、《捷径》。

On screen the Multiprotagonist story is as old as GRAND HOTEL; in the novel older still, War and Peace ; in the theatre older yet, A Midsummer Night’s Dream. Multiprotagonist stories become Multiplot stories. Rather than driving the telling through the focused desire of a protagonist, either single or plural, these works weave a number of smaller stories, each with its own protagonist, to create a dynamic portrait of a specific society.

在银幕上，多主角叙事手法由来已久，例如《大饭店》；在小说中，其历史更为悠久，例如《战争与和平》；在戏剧中，则更为古老，例如《仲夏夜之梦》。多主角叙事逐渐演变为多情节叙事。这类作品并非以单一或多个主角的强烈愿望为叙事主线，而是交织多个小型故事，每个故事都有其自身的主角，从而构建出一幅特定社会的动态图景。

The protagonist need not be human. It may be an animal, BABE, or a cartoon, BUGS BUNNY, or even an inanimate object, such as the hero of the children’s story The Little Engine That Could. Anything that can be given a free will and the capacity to desire, take action, and suffer the consequences can be a protagonist.

主角不一定是人类。它可以是动物，比如小猪宝贝；也可以是卡通人物，比如兔八哥；甚至可以是无生命物体，比如儿童故事《小火车头》中的主人公。任何被赋予自由意志、拥有欲望、行动能力并能承担后果的事物都可以成为主角。

It’s even possible, in rare cases, to switch protagonists halfway through a story. PSYCHO does this, making the shower murder both an emotional and a formal jolt. With the protagonist dead, the audience is momentarily confused; whom is this movie about? The answer is a Plural-Protagonist as the victim’s sister, boyfriend, and a private detective take over the story. But no matter whether the story’s protagonist is single, multi or plural, no matter how he is characterized, all protagonists have certain hallmark qualities, and the first is willpower.

在极少数情况下，甚至可以在故事进行到一半时更换主角。《惊魂记》就采用了这种手法，使得浴室谋杀案既是情感上的冲击，也是形式上的突破。主角死亡后，观众会一时感到困惑：这部电影究竟在讲谁？答案是：这是一部“多元主角”电影，受害者的妹妹、男友和一位私家侦探接过了故事的主导权。但无论故事的主角是单一的、多的还是多元的，无论他/她被如何刻画，所有主角都具有某些共同的特质，而首要的特质就是意志力。

A PROTAGONIST is a willful character.

主角是一个意志坚定的角色。

Other characters may be dogged, even inflexible, but the protagonist in particular is a willful being. The exact quantity of this willpower, however, may not be measurable. A fine story is not necessarily the struggle of a gigantic will versus absolute forces of inevitability. Quality of will is as important as quantity. A protagonist’s willpower may be less than that of the biblical Job, but powerful enough to sustain desire through conflict and ultimately take actions that create meaningful and irreversible change.

其他角色或许固执己见，甚至顽固不化，但主人公尤其意志坚定。然而，这种意志力的确切大小或许难以衡量。一个好的故事未必是意志力与绝对必然性力量的对抗。意志的质量与数量同样重要。主人公的意志力或许不及圣经中的约伯，但足以支撑他在冲突中保持渴望，并最终采取行动，创造意义深远且不可逆转的改变。

What’s more, the true strength of the protagonist’s will may hide behind a passive characterization. Consider Blanche DuBois, protagonist of A STREETCAR NAMED DESIRE. At first glance she seems weak, drifting and will-less , only wanting, she says, to live in reality. Yet beneath her frail characterization, Blanche’s deep character owns a powerful will that drives her unconscious desire: What she really wants is to escape from reality. So Blanche does everything she can to buffer herself against the ugly world that engulfs her: She acts the grand dame, puts doilies on frayed furniture, lampshades on naked light bulbs, tries to make a Prince Charming out of a dullard. When none of this succeeds, she takes the final escape from reality—she goes insane.

更重要的是，主人公真正的意志力可能隐藏在看似被动的性格表象之下。以《欲望号街车》的主人公布兰奇·杜波依斯为例。乍看之下，她似乎软弱无力、漫无目的、意志消沉，她声称自己只想活在现实中。然而，在她脆弱的外表下，布兰奇的内心深处蕴藏着一股强大的意志力，驱使着她潜意识里的渴望：她真正想要的是逃离现实。因此，布兰奇竭尽所能地保护自己，免受这丑陋世界的侵袭：她装腔作势，在破旧的家具上铺上桌布，在裸露的灯泡上套上灯罩，试图把一个笨蛋变成白马王子。当这一切都失败后，她选择了最终逃离现实的方式——精神崩溃。

On the other hand, while Blanche only seems passive, the truly passive protagonist is a regrettably common mistake. A story cannot be told about a protagonist who doesn’t want anything, who cannot make decisions, whose actions effect no change at any level.

另一方面，虽然布兰奇表面上看起来被动，但真正被动的主角却是一个令人遗憾的常见错误。一个什么都不想要、无法做决定、行动在任何层面上都无法产生影响的主角，是无法讲好的故事。

The PROTAGONIST has a conscious desire.

主人公拥有清醒的意识和欲望。

Rather, the protagonist’s will impels a known desire. The protagonist has a need or goal, an object of desire , and knows it. If you could pull your protagonist aside, whisper in his ear, “What do you want?” he would have an answer: “I’d like X today, Y next week, but in the end I want Z.” The protagonist’s object of desire may be external: the destruction of the shark in JAWS, or internal: maturity in BIG. In either case, the protagonist knows what he wants, and for many characters a simple, clear, conscious desire is sufficient.

相反，主人公的意志驱使着一种已知的欲望。主人公有某种需求或目标，一个渴望的对象，并且他对此了然于心。如果你能把主人公拉到一边，在他耳边轻声问：“你想要什么？”他会回答：“我今天想要X，下周想要Y，但最终我想要Z。”主人公渴望的对象可能是外在的：比如《大白鲨》中杀死鲨鱼，也可能是内在的：比如《长大》中的成长。无论哪种情况，主人公都知道自己想要什么，而对于许多角色来说，一个简单、清晰、自觉的欲望就足够了。

The PROTAGONIST may also have a self-contradictory unconscious desire.

主人公也可能存在一种自我矛盾的无意识欲望。

However, the most memorable, fascinating characters tend to have not only a conscious but an unconscious desire. Although these complex protagonists are unaware of their subconscious need, the audience senses it, perceiving in them an inner contradiction. The conscious and unconscious desires of a multidimensional protagonist contradict each other. What he believes he wants is the antithesis of what he actually but unwittingly wants. This is self-evident. What would be the point of giving a character a subconscious desire if it happens to be the very thing he knowingly seeks?

然而，最令人难忘、最引人入胜的角色往往不仅拥有意识层面的欲望，也拥有潜意识层面的欲望。尽管这些复杂的主角并未意识到自身潜意识的需求，但观众却能感受到，并察觉到他们内心的矛盾。多维主角的意识层面和潜意识层面的欲望彼此冲突。他自认为想要的东西，与他实际却无意识地想要的东西截然相反。这一点不言而喻。如果角色潜意识里的欲望恰好是他明知故犯追求的东西，那么赋予他这种潜意识欲望又有何意义呢？

The PROTAGONIST has the capacities to pursue the Object of Desire convincingly.

主人公有能力令人信服地追求心仪的对象。

The protagonist’s characterization must be appropriate. He needs a believable combination of qualities in the right balance to pursue his desires. This doesn’t mean he’ll get what he wants. He may fail. But the character’s desires must be realistic enough in relationship to his will and capacities for the audience to believe that he could be doing what they see him doing and that he has a chance for fulfillment.

主人公的性格塑造必须恰当。他需要具备一系列可信的特质，并且这些特质必须达到恰当的平衡，才能实现自己的愿望。这并不意味着他一定能如愿以偿，他可能会失败。但主人公的愿望必须与其意志和能力相符，这样观众才能相信他有可能做出他们所看到的事情，并且相信他有机会获得满足。

The PROTAGONIST must have at least a chance to attain his desire.

主人公至少应该有机会实现他的愿望。

An audience has no patience for a protagonist who lacks all possibility of realizing his desire. The reason is simple: No one believes this of his own life. No one believes he doesn’t have even the smallest chance of fulfilling his wishes. But if we were to pull the camera back on life, the grand overview might lead us to conclude that, in the words of Henry David Thoreau, “The mass of men lead lives of quiet desperation,” that most people waste their precious time and die with the feeling they’ve fallen short of their dreams. As honest as this painful insight may be, we cannot allow ourselves to believe it. Instead, we carry hope to the end.

观众对一个完全没有可能实现愿望的主人公毫无耐心。原因很简单：没有人会相信自己的人生会如此。没有人会相信自己连实现愿望的希望都渺茫。但如果我们把镜头拉远，审视人生的全貌，或许会得出这样的结论：正如亨利·大卫·梭罗所说，“大多数人过着平静而绝望的生活”，大多数人都在浪费宝贵的时间，最终带着未能实现梦想的遗憾离世。尽管这种痛苦的洞察如此真实，我们却无法接受。相反，我们始终怀抱希望，直至生命的尽头。

Hope, after all, is not unreasonable. It’s simply hypothetical. “If this… if that… if I learn more… if I love more… if I discipline myself… if I win the lottery… if things change, then I’ll have a chance of getting from life what I want.” We all carry hope in our hearts, no matter the odds against us. A protagonist, therefore, who’s literally hopeless, who hasn’t even the minimal capacity to achieve his desire, cannot interest us.

毕竟，希望并非不合理，它只是一种假设。“如果这样……如果那样……如果我学得更多……如果我爱得更多……如果我自律……如果我中了彩票……如果情况有所改变，那么我就有机会得到我想要的生活。”无论胜算多么渺茫，我们心中都怀揣着希望。因此，一个真正绝望、甚至连实现愿望最基本的能力都没有的主人公，是无法引起我们兴趣的。

The PROTAGONIST has the will and capacity to pursue the object of his conscious and/or unconscious desire to the end of the line, to the human limit established by setting and genre.

主人公有意志和能力去追求他有意识或无意识的欲望对象，直到终点，直到达到由背景和类型所设定的人类极限。

The art of story is not about the middle ground, but about the pendulum of existence swinging to the limits, about life lived in its most intense states. We explore the middle ranges of experience, but only as a path to the end of the line. The audience senses that limit and wants it reached. For no matter how intimate or epic the setting, instinctively the audience draws a circle around the characters and their world, a circumference of experience that’s defined by the nature of the fictional reality. This line may reach inward to the soul, outward into the universe, or in both directions at once. The audience, therefore, expects the storyteller to be an artist of vision who can take his story to those distant depths and ranges.

故事的艺术不在于中间地带，而在于存在的钟摆摆动至极限，在于生命体验的极致状态。我们探索体验的中间地带，但这仅仅是通往终点的路径。观众感知到这极限，并渴望抵达它。无论场景多么私密或宏大，观众都会本能地在角色及其世界周围画出一个圆圈，一个由虚构现实的本质所定义的体验范围。这条线可能向内延伸至灵魂，向外延伸至宇宙，或者同时向这两个方向延伸。因此，观众期待讲故事的人是一位具有远见卓识的艺术家，能够将故事带到那些遥远的深度和广度。

A STORY must build to a final action beyond which the audience cannot imagine another.

一个故事必须层层推进，最终达到一个令观众无法想象的结局。

In other words, a film cannot send its audience to the street rewriting it: “Happy ending… but shouldn’t she have settled things with her father? Shouldn’t she have broken up with Ed before she moved in with Mac? Shouldn’t she have…” Or: “Downer… the guy’s dead, but why didn’t he call the cops? And didn’t he keep a gun under the dash, and shouldn’t he have…?” If people exit imagining scenes they thought they should have seen before or after the ending we give them, they will be less than happy moviegoers. We’re supposed to be better writers than they. The audience wants to be taken to the limit, to where all questions are answered, all emotion satisfied—the end of the line.

换句话说，一部电影不能让观众走出影院后还在琢磨剧情：“大团圆结局……但她难道不应该先和她父亲和解吗？她难道不应该在搬去和麦克同住之前就和艾德分手吗？她难道不应该……”或者：“太糟糕了……那家伙死了，但他为什么不报警？他不是在仪表盘下面藏了把枪吗？他难道不应该……？”如果观众看完电影后还在想象着结局前后应该出现的场景，他们就不会感到满意。我们应该比他们更擅长编剧。观众想要的是体验到故事的极致，所有疑问都得到解答，所有情感都得到满足——故事的终点。

The protagonist takes us to this limit. He must have it within himself to pursue his desire to the boundaries of human experience in depth, breadth, or both, to reach absolute and irreversible change. This, by the way, doesn’t mean your film can’t have a sequel; your protagonist may have more tales to tell. It means that each story must find closure for itself.

主人公将我们带到这个极限。他必须拥有足够的内在力量，才能将自己的欲望推向人类经验的边界，无论是在深度上、广度上，还是两者兼具，最终达到绝对且不可逆转的改变。顺便一提，这并不意味着你的电影不能拍续集；你的主人公或许还有更多故事要讲。这只是意味着每个故事都必须有自己的结局。

The PROTAGONIST must be empathetic; he may or may not be sympathetic.

主人公必须有同理心；他可能同情他人，也可能不同情他人。

Sympathetic means likable. Tom Hanks and Meg Ryan, for example, or Spencer Tracy and Katharine Hepburn in their typical roles: The moment they step onscreen, we like them. We’d want them as friends, family members, or lovers. They have an innate likability and evoke sympathy. Empathy, however, is a more profound response.

令人同情意味着讨人喜欢。例如，汤姆·汉克斯和梅格·瑞恩，或者斯宾塞·屈赛和凯瑟琳·赫本在他们典型的角色中：他们一出现在银幕上，我们就喜欢上了他们。我们希望他们成为朋友、家人或爱人。他们天生具有讨人喜欢的特质，能够唤起人们的同情。然而，共情则是一种更为深刻的情感反应。

Empathetic means “like me.” Deep within the protagonist the audience recognizes a certain shared humanity. Character and audience are not alike in every fashion, of course; they may share only a single quality. But there’s something about the character that strikes a chord. In that moment of recognition, the audience suddenly and instinctively wants the protagonist to achieve whatever it is that he desires.

共情意味着“与我相似”。观众在主人公内心深处感受到某种共通的人性。当然，角色和观众并非在所有方面都相同；他们可能只拥有一个共同点。但角色身上总有某种特质能够触动人心。在那一刻，观众会本能地希望主人公能够实现他所渴望的一切。

The unconscious logic of the audience runs like this: “This character is like me. Therefore, I want him to have whatever it is he wants, because if I were he in those circumstances, I’d want the same thing for myself.” Hollywood has many synonymic expressions for this connection: “somebody to get behind,” “someone to root for.” All describe the empathetic connection that the audience strikes between itself and the protagonist. An audience may, if so moved, empathize with every character in your film, but it must empathize with your protagonist. If not, the audience/story bond is broken.

观众的潜意识逻辑是这样的：“这个角色就像我。因此，我希望他能得到他想要的一切，因为如果我处在那种境地，我也会想要同样的东西。”好莱坞有很多表达这种联系的同义词：“值得支持的人”、“值得拥护的人”。这些词语都描述了观众与主角之间建立的共情联系。如果观众被打动，他们可能会对电影中的每个角色都产生共鸣，但他们必须对主角产生共鸣。否则，观众与故事之间的联系就会断裂。

THE AUDIENCE BOND

观众关系

The audience’s emotional involvement is held by the glue of empathy. If the writer fails to fuse a bond between filmgoer and protagonist, we sit outside feeling nothing. Involvement has nothing to do with evoking altruism or compassion. We empathize for very personal, if not egocentric, reasons. When we identify with a protagonist and his desires in life, we are in fact rooting for our own desires in life. Through empathy, the vicarious linking of ourselves to a fictional human being, we test and stretch our humanity. The gift of story is the opportunity to live lives beyond our own, to desire and struggle in a myriad of worlds and times, at all the various depths of our being.

观众的情感投入是由同理心维系的。如果编剧无法在观众和主人公之间建立起联系，我们就会置身事外，毫无感觉。这种投入与激发利他主义或同情心无关。我们产生同理心，往往出于非常个人化，甚至可以说是以自我为中心的理由。当我们认同主人公及其人生愿望时，实际上我们是在为自己人生的愿望加油鼓劲。通过同理心，通过我们与虚构人物的间接联系，我们得以检验和拓展自身的人性。故事的馈赠在于，它让我们有机会体验超越自身人生的经历，在无数个不同的世界和时代中，在我们存在的各种深度，去感受渴望与挣扎。

Empathy, therefore, is absolute, while sympathy is optional. We’ve all met likable people who don’t draw our compassion. A protagonist, accordingly, may or may not be pleasant. Unaware of the difference between sympathy and empathy, some writers automatically devise nice-guy heroes, fearing that if the star role isn’t nice, the audience won’t relate. Uncountable commercial disasters, however, have starred charming protagonists. Likability is no guarantee of audience involvement; it’s merely an aspect of characterization. The audience identifies with deep character, with innate qualities revealed through choice under pressure.

因此，同理心是绝对的，而同情心则是可选的。我们都遇到过一些讨人喜欢却不会引起我们同情的人。相应地，主角可能讨人喜欢，也可能不讨人喜欢。有些作家不了解同情心和同理心的区别，便会不假思索地塑造“好好先生”式的英雄形象，担心如果主角不够讨喜，观众就无法产生共鸣。然而，无数商业失败的作品都以魅力十足的主角为主角。讨人喜欢并不能保证观众投入其中；它仅仅是角色塑造的一个方面。观众会认同那些性格深刻、在压力下通过选择展现出的内在品质的角色。

At first glance creating empathy does not seem difficult. The protagonist is a human being; the audience is full of human beings. As the filmgoer looks up on the screen, he recognizes the character’s humanity, senses that he shares it, identifies with the protagonist, and dives into the story. Indeed, in the hands of the greatest writers, even the most unsympathetic character can be made empathetic.

乍看之下，营造共情似乎并不难。主人公是人，观众也是人。当观众抬头看向银幕时，他们会感受到角色的人性，意识到自己也拥有这种人性，从而与主人公产生共鸣，并沉浸于故事之中。的确，在最伟大的编剧手中，即使是最不讨喜的角色也能令人产生共鸣。

Macbeth, for example, viewed objectively, is monstrous. He butchers a kindly old King while the man is sleeping, a King who had never done Macbeth any harm—in fact, that very day he’d given Macbeth a royal promotion. Macbeth then murders two servants of the King to blame the deed on them. He kills his best friend. Finally he orders the assassination of the wife and infant children of his enemy. He’s a ruthless killer; yet, in Shakespeare’s hands he becomes a tragic, empathetic hero.

例如，客观来看，麦克白是个十足的恶魔。他趁着一位仁慈的老国王熟睡之际将其杀害，这位国王从未伤害过麦克白——事实上，就在当天，国王还提拔了麦克白为王。之后，麦克白又杀害了国王的两名仆人，企图将罪名嫁祸于他们。他还杀死了自己最好的朋友。最后，他下令谋杀了敌人的妻子和幼子。他是个冷酷无情的杀手；然而，在莎士比亚的笔下，他却成为了一个悲剧性的、令人同情的英雄。

The Bard accomplished this feat by giving Macbeth a conscience. As he wanders in soliloquy, wondering, agonizing, “Why am I doing this? What kind of a man am I?” the audience listens and thinks, “What kind? Guilt-ridden… just like me. I feel bad when I’m thinking about doing bad things. I feel awful when I do them and afterward there’s no end to the guilt. Macbeth is a human being; he has a conscience just like mine.” In fact, we’re so drawn to Macbeth’s writhing soul, we feel a tragic loss when at climax Macduff decapitates him. Macbeth is a breathtaking display of the godlike power of the writer to find an empathetic center in an otherwise contemptible character.

莎士比亚赋予麦克白良知，从而成就了这一壮举。当他在独白中徘徊，痛苦地思索着“我为什么要这样做？我究竟是怎样一个人？”时，观众聆听着，心中不禁浮现出这样的疑问：“怎样一个人？充满罪恶感……就像我一样。当我想到要做坏事时，我会感到难过。当我真的做了坏事时，我会感到无比痛苦，事后更是愧疚难耐，永无止境。麦克白是一个有血有肉的人；他和我的一样，也有良知。”事实上，我们如此被麦克白痛苦挣扎的灵魂所吸引，以至于当麦克德夫在剧终斩下他的头颅时，我们感到无比悲痛。麦克白这个角色令人叹为观止地展现了作家神一般的笔力，他能够在一个原本令人鄙夷的角色身上找到令人同情的闪光点。

On the other hand, in recent years many films, despite otherwise splendid qualities, have crashed on these rocks because they failed to create an audience bond. Just one example of many: INTERVIEW WITH A VAMPIRE. The audience’s reaction to Brad Pitt’s Louis went like this: “If I were Louis, caught in his hell-after-death, I’d end it in a flash. Bad luck he’s a vampire. Wouldn’t wish that on anybody. But if he finds it revolting to suck the life out of innocent victims, if he hates himself for turning a child into a devil, if he’s tired of rat blood, he should take this simple solution: Wait for sunrise, and poof, it’s over.” Although Anne Rice’s novel steered us through Louis’s thoughts and feelings until we fell into empathy with him, the dispassionate eye of the camera sees him for what he is, a whining fraud. Audiences always disassociate themselves from hypocrites.

另一方面，近年来许多电影，尽管其他方面都很出色，却因为未能与观众建立情感联系而遭遇滑铁卢。《夜访吸血鬼》就是众多例子之一。观众对布拉德·皮特饰演的路易的反应是这样的：“如果我是路易，被困在死后的地狱里，我会立刻结束这一切。他是个吸血鬼，真倒霉。我可不希望任何人变成那样。但如果他觉得吸食无辜者的生命令人作呕，如果他痛恨自己把孩子变成魔鬼，如果他厌倦了老鼠血，他应该采取这个简单的办法：等到日出，砰！一切就结束了。”尽管安妮·赖斯的小说引导我们了解路易的所思所想，最终让我们对他产生同情，但冷漠的镜头却看穿了他的真面目——一个只会抱怨的骗子。观众总是会与伪君子划清界限。

THE FIRST STEP

第一步

When you sit down to write, the musing begins: “How to start? What would my character do?”

当你坐下来写作时，思考就开始了：“如何开头？我的角色会怎么做？”

Your character, indeed all characters, in the pursuit of any desire, at any moment in story, will always take the minimum, conservative action from his point of view. All human beings always do. Humanity is fundamentally conservative, as indeed is all of nature. No organism ever expends more energy than necessary, risks anything it doesn’t have to, or takes any action unless it must. Why should it? If a task can be done in an easy way without risk of loss or pain, or the expenditure of energy, why would any creature do the more difficult, dangerous, or enervating thing? It won’t. Nature doesn’t allow it… and human nature is just an aspect of universal nature.

你的角色，或者说所有角色，在故事的任何时刻，为了追求任何欲望，都会从自身角度出发，采取最保守、最省力的行动。所有人类都是如此。人性本质上是保守的，正如整个自然界一样。任何生物都不会消耗不必要的能量，不会冒不必要的风险，也不会采取任何迫不得已的行动。它们为什么要这么做呢？如果一项任务可以轻松完成，无需承担任何损失或痛苦，也无需消耗能量，那么任何生物又何必去做更困难、更危险、更耗费精力的事情呢？它们不会。自然不允许这样做……而人性只是普遍自然规律的一个方面。

In life we often see people, even animals, acting with extreme behavior that seems unnecessary, if not stupid. But this is our objective view of their situation. Subjectively, from within the experience of the creature, this apparently intemperate action was minimal, conservative, and necessary. What’s thought “conservative,” after all, is always relative to point of view.

在生活中，我们常常看到人，甚至动物，做出一些看似不必要甚至愚蠢的极端行为。但这只是我们客观上对他们处境的看法。从主观角度来看，从生物自身的体验出发，这种看似过激的行为却是适度的、保守的，甚至是必要的。毕竟，“保守”的定义总是取决于视角。

For example: If a normal person wanted to get into a house, he’d take the minimum and conservative action. He’d knock on the door, thinking, “If I knock, the door’ll be opened. I’ll be invited in and that’ll be a positive step toward my desire.” A martial arts hero, however, as a conservative first step, might karate-chop the door to splinters, feeling that this is prudent and minimal.

例如：如果一个普通人想进屋，他会采取最保守、最基本的行动。他会敲门，心想：“如果我敲门，门就会开。我会被邀请进去，这对我来说是朝着目标迈出的积极一步。”然而，一位武术英雄，作为保守的第一步，可能会用空手道把门劈成碎片，因为他觉得这样做谨慎且适度。

What is necessary but minimal and conservative is relative to the point of view of each character at each precise moment. In life, for example, I say to myself: “If I cross the street now, that car’s far enough away for the driver to see me in time, slow down if needed, and I’ll get across.” Or: “I can’t find Dolores’s phone number. But I know that my friend Jack has it in his Rolodex. If I call him in the midst of his busy day, because he’s my friend, he’ll interrupt what he’s doing and give me the number.”

必要但又精简保守的做法，取决于每个角色在每个特定时刻的视角。例如，在生活中，我会对自己说：“如果我现在过马路，那辆车离得足够远，司机能及时看到我，必要时会减速，我就能安全过马路。”或者：“我找不到多洛雷斯的电话号码。但我知道我的朋友杰克的通讯录里有她的号码。如果我在他忙碌的时候给他打电话，因为他是我的朋友，他肯定会放下手头的事情把号码告诉我。”

In other words, in life we take an action consciously or unconsciously (and life is spontaneous most of the time as we open our mouths or take a step), thinking or sensing within to this effect: “If in these circumstances I take this minimum, conservative action, the world will react to me in a fashion that will be a positive step toward getting me what I want.” And in life, 99 percent of the time we are right. The driver sees you in time, taps the brakes, and you reach the other side safely. You call Jack and apologize for interrupting him. He says, “No problem,” and gives you the number. This is the great mass of experience, hour by hour, in life. BUT NEVER, EVER IN A STORY.

换句话说，在生活中，我们有意或无意地采取行动（而大多数时候，当我们开口说话或迈出一步时，生活都是自发的），内心会这样想或感知：“如果在这种情况下我采取这种最低限度的保守行动，世界将会以一种积极的方式回应我，从而帮助我实现目标。”而在生活中，99%的情况下，我们的判断都是正确的。司机及时看到你，轻踩刹车，你安全到达了对面。你打电话给杰克，为打扰他而道歉。他说：“没关系”，并给了你电话号码。这就是生活中每时每刻的体验。但在故事里，却永远不会出现这种情况。

The grand difference between story and life is that in story we cast out the minutiae of daily existence in which human beings take actions expecting a certain enabling reaction from the world, and, more or less, get what they expect.

故事与生活的最大区别在于，在故事中，我们摒弃了日常生活的琐碎细节，在日常生活中，人们采取行动，期望从世界获得某种促成性的反应，并且或多或少地得到了他们所期望的。

In story, we concentrate on that moment, and only that moment, in which a character takes an action expecting a useful reaction from his world, but instead the effect of his action is to provoke forces of antagonism. The world of the character reacts differently than expected, more powerfully than expected, or both.

在故事中，我们关注的仅仅是这样一个时刻：一个角色采取行动，原本期望从他所处的世界获得有益的回应，但结果却适得其反，激起了敌对势力。角色所处的世界对此作出了出乎意料的反应，反应强度远超预期，或者两者兼而有之。

I pick up the phone, call Jack, and say: “Sorry to bother you, but I can’t find Dolores’s phone number. Could you—” and he shouts: “Dolores? Dolores! How dare you ask me for her number?” and slams down the phone. Suddenly, life is interesting.

我拿起电话，拨通杰克的号码，说道：“不好意思打扰你，但我找不到多洛雷斯的电话号码。你能——”他却吼道：“多洛雷斯？多洛雷斯！你竟敢问我要她的号码？”说完就挂断了电话。突然间，生活变得有趣起来。

THE WORLD OF A CHARACTER

角色世界

This chapter seeks the substance of story as seen from the perspective of a writer who in his imagination has placed himself at the very center of the character he’s creating. The “center” of a human being, that irreducible particularity of the innermost self, is the awareness you carry with you twenty-four hours a day that watches you do everything you do, that chides you when you get things wrong, or compliments you on those rare occasions when you get things right. It’s that deep observer that comes to you when you’re going through the most agonizing experience of your life, collapsed on the floor, crying your heart out… that little voice that says, “Your mascara is running.” This inner eye is you: your identity, your ego, the conscious focus of your being. Everything outside this subjective core is the objective world of a character.

本章从一位作家的视角出发，探寻故事的本质。这位作家在想象中将自己置于所创造角色的中心。“中心”指的是人的内心深处那不可分割的独特之处，它如同你每天24小时都携带的意识，注视着你的一举一动，在你犯错时责备你，在你难得做对时赞扬你。当你经历人生中最痛苦的时刻，瘫倒在地，痛哭流涕时，这个深邃的观察者会来到你身边……那个细小的声音会告诉你：“你的睫毛膏花了。”这双内在的眼睛就是你：你的身份，你的自我，你存在的意识焦点。而在这个主观核心之外的一切，则是角色的客观世界。

A character’s world can be imagined as a series of concentric circles surrounding a core of raw identity or awareness, circles that mark the levels of conflict in a character’s life. The inner circle or level is his own self and conflicts arising from the elements of his nature: mind, body, emotion.

可以将角色的世界想象成一系列围绕着核心原始身份或意识的同心圆，这些圆标志着角色生活中冲突的不同层次。最内层的圆或层次代表着角色的自我，以及源于其本性要素（心智、身体、情感）的冲突。

When, for example, a character takes an action, his mind may not react the way he anticipates. His thoughts may not be as quick, as insightful, as witty as he expected. His body may not react as he imagined. It may not be strong enough or deft enough for a particular task. And we all know how emotions betray us. So the closest circle of antagonism in the world of a character is his own being: feelings and emotions, mind and body, all or any of which may or may not react from one moment to the next the way he expects. As often as not, we are our own worst enemies.

例如，当一个角色采取行动时，他的思维反应可能与预期不符。他的思考可能不如他所预期的那样迅速、敏锐或机智。他的身体反应也可能与他想象的不同。它可能不够强壮或灵活，无法完成特定的任务。我们都知道，情绪会背叛我们。因此，角色世界中最大的敌人就是他自身：感觉和情绪、思维和身体，所有这些，或其中任何一个，都可能在下一刻按照他预期的方式做出反应，也可能完全相反。很多时候，我们最大的敌人就是我们自己。

THE THREE LEVELS OF CONFLICT

冲突的三个层次

The second circle inscribes personal relationships, unions of intimacy deeper than the social role. Social convention assigns the outer roles we play. At the moment, for example, we’re playing teacher/student. Someday, however, our paths may cross and we may decide to change our professional relationship to friendship. In the same manner, parent/child begins as social roles that may or may not go deeper than that. Many of us go through life in parent/child relationships that never deepen beyond social definitions of authority and rebellion. Not until we set the conventional role aside do we find the true intimacy of family, friends, and lovers—who then do not react the way we expect and become the second level of personal conflict.

第二个圆圈描绘的是人际关系，是超越社会角色的深层亲密关系。社会习俗赋予我们外在的角色。例如，此刻我们扮演着师生角色。然而，总有一天，我们的道路会交汇，我们或许会决定将师生关系转变为友谊。同样，父母/子女关系最初也是社会角色，其内涵可能超越社会对权威和反叛的定义。我们许多人一生都处于父母/子女关系中，但这种关系从未超越社会对权威和反叛的定义。只有当我们放下传统角色，才能找到家人、朋友和爱人之间真正的亲密关系——而此时，他们的反应往往出乎我们的意料，从而引发第二层个人冲突。

The third circle marks the level of extra-personal conflict—all the sources of antagonism outside the personal: conflict with social institutions and individuals—government/citizen, church/worshipper; corporation/client; conflict with individuals—cop/criminal/victim, boss/worker, customer/waiter, doctor/patient; and conflict with both man-made and natural environments—time, space, and every object in it.

第三个圆圈标志着超个人冲突的层面——所有个人之外的对抗来源：与社会机构和个人的冲突——政府/公民、教会/信徒、公司/客户；与个人的冲突——警察/罪犯/受害者、老板/员工、顾客/服务员、医生/病人；以及与人造环境和自然环境的冲突——时间、空间及其中的每一个物体。

THE GAP

盖普

STORY is born in that place where the subjective and objective realms touch.

故事诞生于主观与客观交汇之处。

The protagonist seeks an object of desire beyond his reach. Consciously or unconsciously he chooses to take a particular action, motivated by the thought or feeling that this act will cause the world to react in a way that will be a positive step toward achieving his desire. From his subjective point of view the action he has chosen seems minimal, conservative, yet sufficient to effect the reaction he wants. But the moment he takes this action, the objective realm of his inner life, personal relationships, or extra-personal world, or a combination of these, react in a way that’s more powerful or different than he expected.

主人公渴望得到一个遥不可及的目标。他有意识或无意识地选择采取某种行动，其动机源于一种想法或感受：这一行动将促使世界朝着实现他的愿望的方向做出积极的反应。从他的主观视角来看，他选择的行动似乎微不足道、保守，却足以产生他想要的结果。然而，就在他采取这一行动的那一刻，他内心世界、人际关系、外部世界，或三者兼而有之的客观领域，却以一种比他预期更强大或更出乎意料的方式做出了反应。

This reaction from his world blocks his desire, thwarting him and bending him further from his desire than he was before he took this action. Rather than evoking cooperation from his world, his action provokes forces of antagonism that open up the gap between his subjective expectation and the objective result, between what he thought would happen when he took his action and what in fact does happen between his sense of probability and true necessity.

他所处世界的这种反应阻碍了他的愿望，使他受挫，并让他比采取行动之前更加远离自己的愿望。他的行动非但没有赢得世界的合作，反而激起了对抗的力量，拉大了他主观期望与客观结果之间的差距，拉大了他行动时所设想的后果与实际发生的结果之间的差距，拉大了他对可能性的感知与真正必然性之间的差距。

Every human being acts, from one moment to the next, knowingly or unknowingly, on his sense of probability, on what he expects, in all likelihood, to happen when he takes an action. We all walk this earth thinking, or at least hoping, that we understand ourselves, our intimates, society, and the world. We behave according to what we believe to be the truth of ourselves, the people around us, and the environment. But this is a truth we cannot know absolutely. It’s what we believe to be true.

每个人，无论有意无意，都会根据自己的概率感知，根据自己预期采取行动后最有可能发生的情况，做出相应的行动。我们生活在这世上，都认为自己了解自己、了解身边的人、了解社会、了解世界。我们的行为取决于我们对自身、周围的人和环境的认知。但这并非我们绝对了解的真相，而是我们相信的真相。

We also believe we’re free to make any decision whatsoever to take any action whatsoever. But every choice and action we make and take, spontaneous or deliberate, is rooted in the sum total of our experience, in what has happened to us in actuality, imagination, or dream to that moment. We then choose to act based on what this gathering of life tells us will be the probable reaction from our world. It’s only then, when we take action, that we discover necessity.

我们也相信自己有权自由做出任何决定，采取任何行动。但我们所做的每一个选择和采取的每一个行动，无论是自发的还是深思熟虑的，都根植于我们所有经验的总和，根植于我们在此之前在现实、想象或梦境中所经历的一切。然后，我们根据这些人生经历告诉我们，世界可能会做出怎样的反应，来选择行动。只有当我们采取行动时，我们才会发现必要性。

Necessity is absolute truth. Necessity is what in fact happens when we act. This truth is known— and can only be known —when we take action into the depth and breadth of our world and brave its reaction. This reaction is the truth of our existence at that precise moment, no matter what we believed the moment before. Necessity is what must and does actually happen, as opposed to probability, which is what we hope or expect to happen.

必然性是绝对真理。必然性是我们行动后实际发生的结果。只有当我们深入探索世界的广袤与深邃，勇敢面对其反作用时，才能认识到这一真理，也只能认识到这一真理。无论我们前一刻的信念如何，这一反作用力都是我们在那一刻存在的真相。必然性是必须且确实会发生的事，而非概率——概率是我们希望或预期的事。

As in life, so in fiction. When objective necessity contradicts a character’s sense of probability, a gap suddenly cracks open in the fictional reality. This gap is the point where the subjective and objective realms collide, the difference between anticipation and result, between the world as the character perceived it before acting and the truth he discovers in action.

人生亦是如此，小说亦是如此。当客观必然性与人物对概率的感知相悖时，虚构的现实中便会突然出现一道鸿沟。这道鸿沟正是主观与客观领域碰撞之处，是预期与结果之间的差异，是人物行动前所感知的世界与他在行动中发现的真相之间的差距。

Once the gap in reality splits open, the character, being willful and having capacity, senses or realizes that he cannot get what he wants in a minimal, conservative way. He must gather himself and struggle through this gap to take a second action. This next action is something the character would not have wanted to do in the first case because it not only demands more willpower and forces him to dig more deeply into his human capacity, but most important, the second action puts him at risk. He now stands to lose in order to gain.

一旦现实与现实之间的鸿沟被撕裂，这个意志坚定且能力出众的角色便会意识到，他无法以保守的方式轻易获得自己想要的东西。他必须振作起来，努力跨越这道鸿沟，采取第二次行动。这第二次行动是角色在最初情况下不愿做的，因为它不仅需要更强大的意志力，迫使他更深入地挖掘自身的潜能，更重要的是，第二次行动会让他身处险境。他现在面临着为了获得而失去的风险。

ON RISK

风险

We’d all like to have our cake and eat it too. In a state of jeopardy, on the other hand, we must risk something that we want or have in order to gain something else that we want or to protect something we have—a dilemma we strive to avoid.

我们都想鱼与熊掌兼得。然而，在危急情况下，为了获得我们想要的东西或保护我们已经拥有的东西，我们必须冒失去我们想要或已经拥有的东西的风险——这是我们竭力避免的两难境地。

Here’s a simple test to apply to any story. Ask: What is the risk? What does the protagonist stand to lose if he does not get what he wants? More specifically, what’s the worst thing that will happen to the protagonist if he does not achieve his desire?

这里有一个简单的测试方法，适用于任何故事。问问自己：风险是什么？如果主人公没能得到他想要的东西，他会失去什么？更具体地说，如果主人公的愿望没有实现，最糟糕的情况是什么？

If this question cannot be answered in a compelling way, the story is misconceived at its core. For example, if the answer is: “Should the protagonist fail, life would go back to normal,” this story is not worth telling. What the protagonist wants is of no real value, and a story of someone pursuing something of little or no value is the definition of boredom.

如果这个问题无法得到令人信服的解答，那么这个故事从根本上就是错误的。例如，如果答案是：“如果主人公失败了，生活就会恢复正常”，那么这个故事就毫无意义。主人公所追求的东西毫无价值，而一个讲述某人追求微不足道甚至毫无价值之物的故事，正是无聊的代名词。

Life teaches that the measure of the value of any human desire is in direct proportion to the risk involved in its pursuit. The higher the value, the higher the risk. We give the ultimate values to those things that demand the ultimate risks—our freedom, our lives, our souls. This imperative of risk, however, is far more than an aesthetic principle, it’s rooted in the deepest source of our art. For we not only create stories as metaphors for life, we create them as metaphors for meaningful life—and to live meaningfully is to be at perpetual risk.

生活告诉我们，任何人类欲望的价值都与追求它所伴随的风险成正比。价值越高，风险越大。我们赋予那些需要承担最大风险的事物以至高价值——我们的自由、生命、灵魂。然而，这种风险的必然性远不止是一种审美原则，它根植于我们艺术最深层的源泉。因为我们创作故事不仅是为了隐喻人生，更是为了隐喻有意义的人生——而有意义的人生意味着永远处于风险之中。

Examine your own desires. What’s true of you will be true of every character you write. You wish to write for the cinema, the foremost media of creative expression in the world today; you wish to give us works of beauty and meaning that help shape our vision of reality; in return you would like to be acknowledged. It’s a noble ambition and a grand achievement to fulfill. And because you’re a serious artist, you’re willing to risk vital aspects of your life to live that dream.

审视你自身的渴望。你自身的特质，也会体现在你笔下的每一个角色身上。你渴望为电影创作剧本——电影是当今世界最重要的创意表达媒介；你渴望创作出兼具美感与意义的作品，帮助我们塑造对现实的认知；作为回报，你也渴望获得认可。这是一个崇高的抱负，也是一项伟大的成就。正因为你是一位严肃的艺术家，你才愿意为了实现这个梦想而承担生活中至关重要的风险。

You’re willing to risk time. You know that even the most talented writers—Oliver Stone, Lawrence Kasdan, Ruth Prawer Jhabvala—didn’t find success until they were in their thirties or forties, and just as it takes a decade or more to make a good doctor or teacher, it takes ten or more years of adult life to find something to say that tens of millions of people want to hear, and ten or more years and often as many screenplays written and unsold to master this demanding craft.

你愿意投入时间。你知道，即使是最有才华的作家——奥利弗·斯通、劳伦斯·卡斯丹、露丝·普拉沃·贾布瓦拉——也是在三四十岁才获得成功。正如培养一名优秀的医生或教师需要十年甚至更长时间一样，要找到数千万人想听的内容，也需要十年甚至更长时间的成人生活；要掌握这门高要求的技艺，往往需要十年甚至更长时间，以及无数未售出的剧本。

You’re willing to risk money. You know that if you were to take the same hard work and creativity that goes into a decade of unsold screenplays and apply it to a normal profession, you could retire before you see your first script on the screen.

你愿意承担投资风险。你知道，如果你把十年来创作未售剧本所投入的辛勤努力和创造力运用到一份普通的职业中，你可能在看到自己的第一个剧本搬上银幕之前就已经退休了。

You’re willing to risk people. Each morning you go to your desk and enter the imagined world of your characters. You dream and write until the sun’s setting and your head’s throbbing. So you turn off your word processor to be with the person you love. Except that, while you can turn off your machine, you can’t turn off your imagination. As you sit at dinner, your characters are still running through your head and you’re wishing there was a notepad next to your plate. Sooner or later, the person you love will say: “You know… you’re not really here.” Which is true. Half the time you’re somewhere else, and no one wants to live with somebody who isn’t really there.

你愿意冒险。每天早晨，你来到书桌前，进入你笔下人物的想象世界。你沉浸在梦想和写作中，直到夕阳西下，头痛欲裂。于是你关掉电脑，去陪伴你爱的人。然而，你可以关掉电脑，却无法关闭你的想象力。晚餐时，你的人物依然在你脑海中奔涌，你多么希望餐盘旁能放着一个记事本。迟早，你爱的人会说：“你知道吗……你并不真正在这里。” 这话没错。你一半的时间都心不在焉，没有人愿意和一个不在身边的人生活在一起。

The writer places time, money, and people at risk because his ambition has life-defining force. What’s true for the writer is true for every character he creates:

作者之所以将时间、金钱和人置于危险之中，是因为他的抱负具有决定人生走向的力量。对作者而言如此，对他笔下的每一个角色来说也是如此：

The measure of the value of a character’s desire is in direct proportion to the risk he’s willing to take to achieve it; the greater the value, the greater the risk.

衡量一个角色的欲望价值，与他为实现欲望愿意承担的风险成正比；价值越大，风险越大。

THE GAP IN PROGRESSION

进步中的差距

The protagonist’s first action has aroused forces of antagonism that block his desire and spring open a gap between anticipation and result, disconfirming his notions of reality, putting him in greater conflict with his world, at even greater risk. But the resilient human mind quickly remakes reality into a larger pattern that incorporates this disconfirmation, this unexpected reaction. Now he takes a second, more difficult and risk-taking action, an action consistent with his revised vision of reality, an action based on his new expectations of the world. But again his action provokes forces of antagonism, splitting open a gap in his reality. So he adjusts to the unexpected, ups the ante yet again and decides to take an action that he feels is consistent with his amended sense of things. He reaches even more deeply into his capacities and willpower, puts himself at greater risk, and takes a third action.

主人公的第一个行动激起了对抗的力量，阻碍了他的愿望，并在预期与结果之间撕开了一道鸿沟，否定了他对现实的认知，使他与世界的冲突加剧，身处更大的风险之中。然而，人类坚韧的思维迅速将现实重塑成一个更大的模式，将这种否定和意外的反应纳入其中。现在，他采取了第二个行动，一个更加艰难且风险更高的行动，一个与他修正后的现实观相符的行动，一个基于他对世界的新预期的行动。但他的行动再次激起了对抗的力量，在他心中的现实中撕开了一道裂缝。于是，他调整自己以适应意外，再次加大赌注，决定采取一个他认为与他修正后的认知相符的行动。他更加深入地挖掘自身的能力和意志力，将自己置于更大的风险之中，并采取了第三个行动。

Perhaps this action achieves a positive result, and for the moment he takes a step toward his desire, but with his next action, the gap will again spring open. Now he must take an even more difficult action that demands even more willpower, more capacity, and more risk. Over and over again in a progression, rather than cooperation, his actions provoke forces of antagonism, opening gaps in his reality. This pattern repeats on various levels to the end of the line, to a final action beyond which the audience cannot imagine another.

或许这一举动能带来积极的结果，让他暂时朝着愿望迈进了一步，但随着下一步行动的展开，差距又会再次扩大。现在他必须采取更加艰难的行动，这需要更强的意志力、更大的能力和更大的风险。他的行动一次又一次地引发对抗，而非合作，从而在他现实中撕开一道道裂缝。这种模式在各个层面不断重复，直至终点，直至观众无法想象的最终行动。

These cracks in moment-to-moment reality mark the difference between the dramatic and the prosaic, between action and activity. True action is physical, vocal, or mental movement that opens gaps in expectation and creates significant change. Mere activity is behavior in which what is expected happens, generating either no change or trivial change.

这些瞬息万变的现实裂缝，标志着戏剧性与平淡无奇、行动与活动之间的区别。真正的行动是身体、言语或心理上的运动，它打破了预期，创造了意义深远的改变。而仅仅是活动，其结果都在预期之内，要么没有改变，要么只带来了微不足道的改变。

But the gap between expectation and result is far more than a matter of cause and effect. In the most profound sense, the break between the cause as it seemed and the effect as it turns out marks the point where the human spirit and the world meet. On one side is the world as we believe it to be, on the other is reality as it actually is. In this gap is the nexus of story, the caldron that cooks our tellings. Here the writer finds the most powerful, life-bending moments. The only way we can reach this crucial junction is by working from the inside out.

但期望与结果之间的差距远不止是因果关系那么简单。从最深刻的意义上讲，看似的原因与最终的结果之间的断裂，标志着人类精神与世界的交汇点。一边是我们所相信的世界，另一边是它实际存在的样子。故事的交汇点，是孕育我们讲述故事的熔炉。在这里，作家找到了最有力、最能改变人生的瞬间。而我们抵达这个关键节点的唯一途径，就是从内在出发，由内而外地进行探索。

WRITING FROM THE INSIDE OUT

由内而外地写作

Why must we do this? Why during the creation of a scene must we find our way to the center of each character and experience it from his point of view? What do we gain when we do? What do we sacrifice if we don’t?

我们为什么要这样做？为什么在创作场景时，我们必须找到每个角色的核心，并从他的角度去体验？这样做我们能获得什么？如果不这样做，我们又会失去什么？

Like anthropologists, we could, for example, discover social and environmental truths through careful observations. Like note-taking psychologists, we could find behavioral truths. We could, by working from the outside in, render a surface of character that’s genuine, even fascinating. But the one crucial dimension we would not create is emotional truth.

例如，我们可以像人类学家一样，通过细致的观察发现社会和环境方面的真相；像做笔记的心理学家一样，发现行为方面的真相；我们可以从外部视角出发，塑造出真实甚至引人入胜的人物形象。但我们无法创造的一个关键维度是情感真相。

The only reliable source of emotional truth is yourself. If you stay outside your characters, you inevitably write emotional clichés. To create revealing human reactions, you must not only get inside your character, but get inside yourself. So, how to do this? How, as you sit at your desk, do you crawl inside the head of your character to feel your heart pounding, your palms sweating, a knot in your belly, tears in your eyes, laughter in your heart, sexual arousal, anger, outrage, compassion, sadness, joy, or any of the uncountable responses along the spectrum of human emotions?

情感真相的唯一可靠来源是你自己。如果你置身事外，无法真正理解笔下人物，那么你写出的必然是情感上的陈词滥调。要塑造出真实动人的人性反应，你不仅要深入角色内心，更要深入自身内心。那么，该如何做到这一点呢？当你坐在书桌前，如何才能真正设身处地地感受角色的心跳、手心冒汗、胃里翻江倒海、眼眶湿润、内心涌起欢笑、性欲高涨、愤怒、愤慨、同情、悲伤、喜悦，或者其他任何一种人类情感的丰富层次呢？

You’ve determined that a certain event must take place in your story, a situation to be progressed and turned. How to write a scene of insightful emotions? You could ask: How should someone take this action? But that leads to clichés and moralizing. Or you could ask: How might someone do this? But that leads to writing “cute”—clever but dishonest. Or: “If my character were in these circumstances, what would he do?” But that puts you at a distance, picturing your character walking the stage of his life, guessing at his emotions, and guesses are invariably clichés. Or you could ask: “If I were in these circumstances, what would I do?” As this question plays on your imagination, it may start your heart pounding, but obviously you’re not the character. Although it may be an honest emotion for you, your character might do the reverse. So what do you do?

你已经确定故事中必须发生某个事件，需要推进剧情发展。那么，如何才能写出一个充满深刻情感的场景呢？你可以问自己：一个人应该如何采取这个行动？但这会导致陈词滥调和说教。或者你可以问：一个人可能会怎么做？但这会导致写出“可爱”——机智却不真诚。又或者：“如果我的角色身处这种境地，他会怎么做？”但这会让你与角色保持距离，想象着角色走在他的人生舞台上，猜测他的情感，而猜测总是落入俗套。或者你可以问：“如果我身处这种境地，我会怎么做？”这个问题可能会让你心跳加速，但显然你不是角色。虽然这可能是你内心真实的情感，但你的角色可能会做出相反的选择。那么，你该怎么办呢？

You ask: “If I were this character in these circumstances, what would I do?” Using Stanislavski’s “Magic if,” you act the role. It is no accident that many of the greatest playwrights from Euripides to Shakespeare to Pinter, and screenwriters from D. W. Griffith to Ruth Gordon to John Sayles were also actors. Writers are improvisationalists who perform sitting at their word processors, pacing their rooms, acting all their characters: man, woman, child, monster. We act in our imaginations until honest, character-specific emotions flow in our blood. When a scene is emotionally meaningful to us, we can trust that it’ll be meaningful to the audience. By creating work that moves us, we move them.

你会问：“如果我是这个角色，身处这样的境地，我会怎么做？”运用斯坦尼斯拉夫斯基的“如果”表演法，你就可以扮演这个角色。从欧里庇得斯到莎士比亚再到品特，许多最伟大的剧作家，以及从D·W·格里菲斯到露丝·戈登再到约翰·塞尔斯的编剧，同时也是演员，这绝非偶然。作家是即兴表演者，他们坐在电脑前，在房间里踱步，演绎着他们笔下的所有角色：男人、女人、孩子、怪物。我们在想象中表演，直到真挚的、与角色相关的情感流淌在我们的血液里。当一个场景对我们而言充满情感意义时，我们就能相信它对观众也同样意义非凡。通过创作能够打动我们的作品，我们也能打动他们。

CHINATOWN

唐人街

To illustrate writing from the inside out, I’ll use one of the most famous and brilliantly written scenes in film, the second act climax of CHINATOWN by screenwriter Robert Towne. I’ll work from the scene as performed on screen, but it can also be found in the third draft of Towne’s screenplay, dated October 9, 1973.

为了阐释由内而外的写作方法，我将以电影史上最著名、最精彩的场景之一——编剧罗伯特·汤恩的《唐人街》第二幕高潮部分为例。我将以电影中的呈现方式进行分析，但这一场景也可以在汤恩1973年10月9日完成的第三稿剧本中找到。

Synopsis

概要

Private detective J. J. Gittes is investigating the death of Hollis Mulwray, commissioner of the Los Angeles Department of Water and Power. Mulwray has apparently drowned in a reservoir, and the crime baffles Gittes’s rival, Police Lieutenant Escobar. Near the end of the Act Two, Gittes has narrowed suspects and motives to two: either a conspiracy of millionaires led by the ruthless Noah Cross killed Mulwray for political power and riches; or Evelyn Mulwray killed her husband in a jealous rage after he was found with another woman.

私家侦探J·J·吉特斯正在调查洛杉矶水电局局长霍利斯·穆尔雷的死因。穆尔雷显然溺死在水库中，这起案件令吉特斯的竞争对手，警官埃斯科巴百思不得其解。第二幕接近尾声时，吉特斯将嫌疑人和作案动机缩小到两种可能：要么是以冷酷无情的诺亚·克罗斯为首的一群百万富翁为了政治权力和财富而谋杀了穆尔雷；要么是伊芙琳·穆尔雷在丈夫被发现与另一名女子在一起后，出于嫉妒而将其杀害。

Gittes follows Evelyn to a house in Santa Monica. Peering through a window, he sees the “other woman,” seemingly drugged and held prisoner. When Evelyn comes out to her car, he forces her to talk and she claims that the woman is her sister. Gittes knows she doesn’t have a sister, but for the moment says nothing.

吉特斯跟踪伊芙琳来到圣莫尼卡的一栋房子。他透过窗户看到“另一个女人”，似乎被下了药，被囚禁着。伊芙琳走到车旁后，吉特斯强迫她开口，她声称那个女人是她的妹妹。吉特斯知道她没有妹妹，但暂时什么也没说。

The next morning he discovers what appears to be the dead man’s eyeglasses in a salt water pond at the Mulwray home in the hills above L.A. Now he knows how and where the man was killed. With this evidence he goes back to Santa Monica to confront Evelyn and turn her over to Escobar, who’s threatening to pull Gittes’s private investigator’s license.

第二天早上，他在洛杉矶山上穆尔雷家的咸水池塘里发现了一副疑似死者的眼镜。现在他知道了死者的死因和地点。带着这条证据，他回到圣莫尼卡，去找伊芙琳对质，并把她交给埃斯科巴。埃斯科巴威胁要吊销吉特斯的私家侦探执照。

CHARACTERS

人物

J.J. GITTES, while working for the district attorney, fell in love with a woman in Chinatown and while trying to help her somehow caused her death. He resigned and became a PI, hoping to escape corrupt politics and his tragic past. But now he’s drawn back into both. What’s worse, he finds himself in this predicament because, days before the murder, he was duped into investigating Mulwray for adultery. Someone’s made a fool of Gittes and he’s a man of excessive pride. Behind his cool demeanor is an impulsive risk-taker; his sarcastic cynicism masks an idealist’s hunger for justice. To further complicate matters, he’s fallen in love with Evelyn Mulwray. Gittes’s scene objective: to find the truth.

J.J. 吉特斯在地方检察官办公室工作期间，爱上了唐人街的一位女子。在试图帮助她时，却意外地导致了她的死亡。他辞职成为一名私家侦探，希望摆脱腐败的政治和悲惨的过去。然而，如今他却再次被卷入其中。更糟糕的是，就在谋杀案发生前几天，他被骗去调查穆尔雷的通奸案，这让他陷入了如今的困境。有人戏弄了吉特斯，而他生性骄傲。他冷静的外表下隐藏着一颗冲动冒险的心；他讽刺挖苦的外表下，隐藏着一颗渴望正义的理想主义者的心。雪上加霜的是，他爱上了伊芙琳·穆尔雷。吉特斯的任务目标：找出真相。

EVELYN MULWRAY is the victim’s wife and daughter of Noah Cross. She’s nervous and defensive when questioned about her husband; she stammers when her father is mentioned. She is, we sense, a woman with something to hide. She has hired Gittes to look into the murder of her husband, perhaps to conceal her own guilt. During the investigation, however, she seems drawn to him. After a close escape from some thugs, they make love. Evelyn’s scene objective: to hide her secret and escape with Katherine.

伊芙琳·穆尔雷是受害者的妻子，也是诺亚·克罗斯的女儿。当被问及丈夫时，她显得紧张而防备；提到父亲时，她更是结结巴巴。我们感觉她似乎有所隐瞒。她雇佣吉特斯调查丈夫的谋杀案，或许是为了掩盖自己的罪行。然而，在调查过程中，她似乎被吉特斯吸引。在一次险些被暴徒抓获后，两人发生了关系。伊芙琳此行的目的：隐藏自己的秘密，并带着凯瑟琳逃走。

KHAN is Evelyn’s servant. Now that she’s widowed, he also sees himself as her bodyguard. He prides himself on his dignified manner and ability to handle difficult situations. Khan’s scene objective: to protect evelyn.

可汗是伊芙琳的仆人。如今她成了寡妇，他也把自己视为她的保镖。他以自己高贵的举止和处理棘手情况的能力而自豪。可汗的本场任务：保护伊芙琳。

KATHERINE is a shy innocent who has lead a very protected life. Katherine’s scene objective: to obey evelyn.

凯瑟琳是一个害羞天真的女孩，从小过着被保护得很好的生活。凯瑟琳的场景目标：服从伊芙琳。

To work from the inside out, slip in Gittes’ mind while he drives to Evelyn’s hideaway. Imagine yourself in Gittes’ pov. As the streets roll past, you ask:

“If I were Gittes at this moment, what would I do?”

“如果我是吉特斯，我会怎么做？”

Letting your imagination roam, the answer comes:

“Rehearse. I always rehearse in my head before taking on life’s big confrontations.”

“预演。在面对人生中的重大挑战之前，我总是会在脑海中进行预演。”

Now work deeper into Gittes’s emotions and psyche:

现在深入探究吉特斯的情感和心理：

Hands white-knuckled on the steering wheel, thoughts racing: “She killed him, then used me. She lied to me, came on to me. Man, I fell for her. My guts are in a knot, but I’ll be cool. I’ll stroll to the door, step in and accuse her. She lies. I send for the cops. She plays innocent, a few tears. But I stay ice cold, show her Mulwray’s glasses, then lay out how she did it, step by step, as if I was there. She confesses. I turn her over to Escobar; I’m off the hook.”

双手紧紧握着方向盘，指节泛白，思绪万千：“她杀了他，然后利用了我。她骗我，勾引我。唉，我竟然爱上她了。我心乱如麻，但我必须保持冷静。我会走到门口，走进去，指控她。她撒谎。我叫警察。她装无辜，流了几滴眼泪。但我依然冷若冰霜，给她看穆尔雷的眼镜，然后一步一步地把她是怎么做的，就好像我亲眼所见一样。她认罪了。我把她交给埃斯科巴；我就脱罪了。”

This is the location of a critical rewrite. In the third draft Evelyn explains at great length that her mother died when she was fifteen and her father’s grief was such that he had a “breakdown” and became “a little boy,” unable to feed or dress himself. This led to incest between them. Unable to face what he had done, her father then turned his back on her. This exposition not only slowed the pace of the scene, but more importantly, it seriously weakened the power of the antagonist, giving him a sympathetic vulnerability. It was cut and replaced by Gittes’ “He raped you?” and Evelyn’s denial—a brilliant stroke that maintains Cross’s cruel core, and severely tests Gittes’ love for Evelyn.

这是关键性修改之处。在第三稿中，伊芙琳用了大量篇幅解释她十五岁时母亲去世，父亲悲痛欲绝，精神崩溃，变得像个“小男孩”，连吃饭穿衣都做不到。这导致了父子乱伦。父亲无法面对自己的所作所为，最终与她断绝了关系。这段描述不仅拖慢了场景节奏，更重要的是，它严重削弱了反派的威慑力，使他显得脆弱而令人同情。这段被删去，取而代之的是吉特斯的“他强奸了你？”以及伊芙琳的否认——这一巧妙的改动既保留了克罗斯残酷的本质，又严峻地考验了吉特斯对伊芙琳的爱。

This opens at least two possible explanations for why Evelyn denies she was raped: Children often have a self-destructive need to protect their parents. It could well have been rape, but even now she cannot bring herself to accuse her father. Or was she complicit. Her mother was dead, making her the “woman of the house.” In those circumstances, incest between father and daughter is not unknown. That, however, doesn’t excuse Cross. The responsibility is his in either case, but Evelyn has punished herself with guilt. Her denial forces Gittes to face character defining choices: whether or not to continue loving this woman, whether or not to turn her over to the police for murder. Her denial contradicts his expectation and a void opens:

这至少为伊芙琳否认自己被强奸提供了两种可能的解释：孩子往往有一种自我毁灭的本能，想要保护父母。这很可能就是强奸，但即使到了现在，她也无法让自己指控父亲。或者，她是否是同谋？她的母亲已经去世，她成了“家里的女主人”。在这种情况下，父女乱伦并非罕见。然而，这并不能为克罗斯开脱。无论哪种情况，责任都在他，但伊芙琳却因此饱受内疚的折磨。她的否认迫使吉特斯面临一个关乎他性格的抉择：是否继续爱着这个女人，是否将她交给警方以谋杀罪名起诉。她的否认与他的预期相悖，一个空洞就此出现：

CREATING WITHIN THE GAP

在差距中创造

In writing out what actors call “inner monologues” I’ve put this well-paced scene into ultra-slow motion, and given words to what would be flights of feeling or flashes of insight. Nonetheless, that’s how it is at the desk. It may take days, even weeks, to write what will be minutes, perhaps seconds, on screen. We put each and every moment under a microscope of thinking, rethinking, creating, recreating as we weave through our characters’ moments, a maze of unspoken thoughts, images, sensations, and emotions.

在创作演员所谓的“内心独白”时，我将原本节奏流畅的场景放慢速度，用文字描绘出那些原本可能只是情感的爆发或灵光乍现的瞬间。然而，这就是剧本创作的本质。写出最终呈现在银幕上可能只需几分钟甚至几秒钟的台词，可能需要数天甚至数周的时间。我们如同用显微镜观察每一个瞬间，反复思考、创作、再创作，最终将角色的每一个时刻——一个由未言明的思绪、画面、感觉和情感交织而成的迷宫——编织成一幅生动的画面。

Writing from the inside out, however, does not mean that we imagine a scene from one end to the other locked in a single character’s point of view. Rather, as in the exercise above, the writer shifts points of view. He settles into the conscious center of a character and asks the question: “If I were this character in these circumstances, what would I do?” He feels within his own emotions a specific human reaction and imagines the character’s next action.

然而，从内而外地写作并不意味着我们完全按照单一角色的视角来想象整个场景。相反，正如上面的练习所示，作者会转换视角。他进入角色的意识中心，并提出这样的问题：“如果我是这个角色，身处这样的境地，我会怎么做？”他感受自身情感中特定的人类反应，并想象角色接下来的行动。

Now the writer’s problem is this: how to progress the scene? To build a next beat, the writer must move out of the character’s subjective point of view and take an objective look at the action he just created. This action anticipates a certain reaction from the character’s world. But that must not occur. Instead, the writer must pry open the gap. To do so, he asks the question writers have been asking themselves since time began: “What is the opposite of that?”

现在，作者面临的问题是：如何推进剧情发展？为了构建下一个节奏，作者必须跳出角色的主观视角，客观地审视他刚刚创造的事件。这个事件预示着角色所处世界会产生某种反应。但这种反应不应该发生。相反，作者必须打破这种僵局。为此，他要问自己一个自古以来作家们就一直在思考的问题：“它的反面是什么？”

Writers are by instinct dialectical thinkers. As Jean Cocteau said, “The spirit of creation is the spirit of contradiction—the breakthrough of appearances toward an unknown reality.” You must doubt appearances and seek the opposite of the obvious. Don’t skim the surface, taking things at face value. Rather, peel back the skin of life to find the hidden, the unexpected, the seemingly inappropriate—in other words, the truth. And you will find your truth in the gap.

作家天生就是辩证思考者。正如让·科克托所说：“创作的精神就是矛盾的精神——突破表象，探寻未知的真相。” 你必须质疑表象，探寻显而易见的反面。不要流于表面，只看表面。相反，要层层剥开生活的表象，去发现隐藏的、意想不到的、看似不合时宜的——换句话说，就是真相。你会在缝隙中找到属于你的真相。

Remember, you are the God of your universe. You know your characters, their minds, bodies, emotions, relationships, world. Once you’ve created an honest moment from one point of view, you move around your universe, even into the inanimate, looking for another point of view so you can invade that, create an unexpected reaction, and splinter open the cleft between expectation and result.

记住，你是你宇宙的神。你了解你的角色，他们的思想、身体、情感、人际关系以及他们所处的世界。一旦你从一个视角创造了一个真实的瞬间，你就可以在你的宇宙中穿梭，甚至进入无生命的事物，寻找另一个视角，以便介入其中，引发意想不到的反应，并撕开预期与结果之间的裂痕。

Having done this, you then go back into the mind of the first character, and find your way to a new emotional truth by asking again: “If I were this character under these new circumstances, what would I do?” Finding your way to that reaction and action, you then step right out again, asking: “And what is the opposite of that?”

完成这一步后，你再回到第一个角色的内心世界，通过再次提问来找到新的情感真相：“如果我是这个角色，在这种新情况下我会怎么做？”找到这种反应和行动后，你再跳出这个角色，问：“那么，与此相反的情况是什么？”

Fine writing emphasizes REACTIONS.

优秀的写作注重表现反应。

Many of the actions in any story are more or less expected. By genre convention, the lovers in a Love Story will meet, the detective in a Thriller will discover a crime, the protagonist’s life in an Education Plot will bottom out. These and other such commonplace actions are universally known and anticipated by the audience. Consequently, fine writing puts less stress on what happens than on to whom it happens and why and how it happens. Indeed, the richest and most satisfying pleasures of all are found in stories that focus on the reactions that events cause and the insight gained.

任何故事中的许多情节或多或少都在意料之中。按照类型片的惯例，爱情故事中的恋人会相遇，惊悚片中的侦探会发现罪案，教育题材作品中的主人公会遭遇人生低谷。这些以及其他类似的常见情节，观众普遍了解并有所预期。因此，优秀的写作并不着重于“发生了什么”，而是更关注“发生在谁身上”、“为什么发生”以及“如何发生”。事实上，最丰富、最令人满足的乐趣，往往来自于那些聚焦于事件引发的反应以及由此获得的感悟的故事。

Looking back at the CHINATOWN scene: Gittes knocks on the door expecting to be let in. What’s the reaction he gets? Khan blocks his way, expecting Gittes to wait. Gittes’s reaction? He shocks Khan by insulting him in Cantonese and barging in. Evelyn comes downstairs expecting Gittes’s help. The reaction to that? Gittes calls the police, expecting to force her to confess the murder and tell the truth about the “other woman.” Reaction? She reveals that the other woman is her daughter by incest, indicting her lunatic father for the murder. Beat after beat, even in the quietest, most internalized of scenes, a dynamic series of action/ reaction /gap, renewed action/surprising reaction /gap builds the scene to and around its Turning Point as reactions amaze and fascinate.

回顾唐人街那一幕：吉特斯敲门，本以为会被放进去。结果如何？可汗挡住了他的去路，以为吉特斯会等着。吉特斯的反应呢？他用粤语辱骂可汗，然后闯了进去，这让可汗大吃一惊。伊芙琳下楼来，指望吉特斯帮忙。结果呢？吉特斯打电话报警，想逼她承认谋杀，并说出“另一个女人”的真相。结果呢？她透露，那个女人是她乱伦所生的女儿，并指控她精神失常的父亲是凶手。一幕幕，即使在最安静、最内敛的场景中，一系列动态的行动/反应/停顿，以及再次的行动/出人意料的反应/停顿，层层推进，最终汇聚到转折点，而观众的反应也令人惊叹，引人入胜。

If you write a beat in which a character steps up to a door, knocks, and waits, and in reaction the door is politely opened to invite him in, and the director is foolish enough to shoot this, in all probability it will never see the light of the screen. Any editor worthy of the title would instantly scrap it, explaining to the director: “Jack, these are eight dead seconds. He knocks on the door and it’s actually opened for him? No, we’ll cut to the sofa. That’s the first real beat. Sorry you squandered fifty thousand dollars walking your star through a door, but it’s a pace killer and pointless.” A “pointless pace killer” is any scene in which reactions lack insight and imagination, forcing expectation to equal result.

如果你写了一个场景，一个角色走到门前，敲门，然后等待，门被礼貌地打开邀请他进去，而导演又傻到把这拍了下来，那这个场景很可能永远不会出现在银幕上。任何一个称职的剪辑师都会立刻把它删掉，并向导演解释：“杰克，这八秒钟毫无意义。他敲门，门真的开了？不行，我们直接切到沙发上。那才是第一个真正的场景。很遗憾你浪费了五万美元让你的明星走进门，但这完全破坏了节奏，毫无意义。” 所谓“毫无意义的节奏杀手”，指的是任何缺乏洞察力和想象力的场景，它强迫观众的预期与结果完全一致。

Once you’ve imagined the scene, beat by beat, gap by gap, you write. What you write is a vivid description of what happens and the reactions it gets, what is seen, said, and done. You write so that when someone else reads your pages he will, beat by beat, gap by gap, live through the roller coaster of life that you lived through at your desk. The words on the page allow the reader to plunge into each gap, seeing what you dreamed, feeling what you felt, learning what you understood until, like you, the reader’s pulse pounds, emotions flow, and meaning is made.

一旦你将场景逐一构思好，逐帧逐句地描绘出来，你就可以开始写作了。你所写的是对所发生之事及其引发的反应的生动描述，是对所见、所言、所行的描绘。你写作的目的是，当别人阅读你的文字时，他们也能逐帧逐句地体验你坐在书桌前经历的人生过山车。纸上的文字让读者能够沉浸于每一个空白之中，看到你梦见的景象，感受到你感受的情绪，领悟你领悟的道理，直到他们也像你一样，心跳加速，情感涌动，最终领悟到其中的意义。

THE SUBSTANCE AND ENERGY OF STORY

故事的实质与能量

The answers to the questions that began this chapter should now be clear. The stuff of a story is not its words. Your text must be lucid to express the desk-bound life of your imagination and feelings. But words are not an end, they are a means, a medium. The substance of story is the gap that splits open between what a human being expects to happen when he takes an action and what really does happen; the rift between expectation and result, probability and necessity. To build a scene, we constantly break open these breaches in reality.

本章开头提出的问题，现在应该都有了答案。故事的本质并非在于文字。你的文字必须清晰流畅，才能表达你伏案构思的想象力和情感。但文字本身并非目的，而是一种手段，一种媒介。故事的实质，在于人类采取行动时所预期的结果与实际发生的结果之间的差距；在于预期与结果、可能性与必然性之间的裂痕。为了构建场景，我们不断地在现实中撕开这些裂缝。

As to the source of energy in story, the answer is the same: the gap. The audience empathizes with the character, vicariously seeking his desire. It more or less expects the world to react the way the character expects. When the gap opens up for character, it opens up for audience. This is the “Oh, my God!” moment, the “Oh, no!” or “Oh, yes!” you’ve experienced again and again in well-crafted stories.

至于故事能量的来源，答案始终如一：那就是差距。观众会与角色产生共鸣，感同身受地体验他的渴望。他们或多或少地期待着世界会按照角色的预期做出反应。当角色的差距出现时，观众的差距也随之出现。这就是你在精心构思的故事中反复体验到的“我的天哪！”、“哦，不！”或“哦，太好了！”的时刻。

The next time you go to the movies, sit in the front row at the wall, so you can watch an audience watch a film. It’s very instructive: Eyebrows fly up, mouths drop open, bodies flinch and rock, laughter explodes, tears run down faces. Every time the gap splits open for character, it opens for audience. With each turn, the character must pour more energy and effort into his next action. The audience, in empathy with the character, feels the same surges of energy building beat by beat through the film.

下次你去电影院，不妨坐在靠墙的第一排，这样你就能观察观众的反应。这很有启发性：他们会惊讶地扬起眉毛，张大嘴巴，身体不由自主地颤抖摇晃，爆发出阵阵笑声，甚至有人热泪盈眶。每当角色情绪爆发，观众的感受也会随之释放。随着剧情的推进，角色必须投入更多的精力和努力才能完成下一步动作。观众与角色产生共鸣，也能感受到影片中同样的能量波动，随着剧情的推进，能量也随之不断积聚。

As a charge of electricity leaps from pole to pole in a magnet, so the spark of life ignites across the gap between the self and reality. With this flash of energy we ignite the power of story and move the heart of the audience.

如同磁铁中电荷在两极间跃动，生命的火花也点燃了自我与现实之间的鸿沟。凭借这股能量的闪光，我们点燃故事的力量，触动观众的心灵。

#↩

8
THE INCITING INCIDENT

8 诱发事件

A story is a design in five parts: The Inciting Incident , the first major event of the telling, is the primary cause for all that follows, putting into motion the other four elements— Progressive Complications, Crisis, Climax, Resolution. To understand how the Inciting Incident enters into and functions within the work, let’s step back to take a more comprehensive look at setting , the physical and social world in which it occurs.

故事的结构由五个部分组成：诱发事件，即故事叙述中的第一个重大事件，是后续一切发展的根本原因，它推动了其他四个要素——渐进式复杂化、危机、高潮和结局——的展开。为了理解诱发事件如何融入故事并发挥作用，让我们退后一步，更全面地审视一下故事发生的背景，即它所处的物质和社会环境。

THE WORLD OF THE STORY

故事的世界

We’ve defined setting in terms of period, duration, location, and level of conflict. These four dimensions frame the story’s world, but to inspire the multitude of creative choices you need to tell an original , cliché-free story, and you must fill that frame with a depth and breadth of detail. Below is a list of general questions we ask of all stories. Beyond these, each work inspires a unique list of its own, driven by the writer’s thirst for insight.

我们从时代背景、故事时长、地点和冲突程度四个方面定义了故事设定。这四个维度构成了故事的世界，但要激发丰富的创作灵感，你需要讲述一个原创且不落俗套的故事，并且必须用详尽而深刻的细节来填充这个框架。以下是我们向所有故事提出的一些通用问题。除此之外，每部作品都会激发出一份独一无二的问题清单，这源于作者对洞察力的渴望。

How do my characters make a living? We spend a third or more of our lives at work, yet rarely see scenes of people doing their jobs. The reason is simple: Most work is boring. Perhaps not to the person doing the work, but boring to watch. As any lawyer, cop, or doctor knows, the vast majority of their time is spent in routine duties, reports, and meetings that change little or nothing—the epitome of expectation meeting result. That’s why in the professional genres— Courtroom, Crime, Medical —we focus on only those moments when work causes more problems than it solves. Nonetheless, to get inside a character, we must question all aspects of their twenty-four-hour day. Not only work, but how do they play? Pray? Make love?

我的角色是如何谋生的？我们一生中至少有三分之一的时间都在工作，却很少看到人们工作时的场景。原因很简单：大多数工作都很枯燥。或许对工作者而言并非如此，但对旁观者来说却很乏味。任何律师、警察或医生都知道，他们绝大部分时间都耗费在例行公事、报告和会议上，这些工作几乎毫无改变——这正是预期与结果完全一致的典型例子。因此，在专业题材作品中——法庭、犯罪、医疗——我们只关注工作带来的问题多于解决的问题。然而，要想真正了解一个角色，我们必须探究他们一天24小时的方方面面。不仅是工作，还有他们的娱乐方式、祈祷方式以及性生活。

What are the politics of my world? Not necessarily politics in terms of right-wing/left-wing, Republican/Democrat, but in the true sense of the word: power. Politics is the name we give to the orchestration of power in any society. Whenever human beings gather to do anything, there’s always an uneven distribution of power. In corporations, hospitals, religions, government agencies, and the like, someone at the top has great power, people at the bottom have little or none, those in between have some. How does a worker gain power or lose it? No matter how we try to level inequalities, applying egalitarian theories of all kinds, human societies are stubbornly and inherently pyramidal in their arrangement of power. In other words, politics.

我的世界里的政治是什么？这里说的政治并非指左右翼、共和党/民主党之分，而是其真正意义上的权力。政治是我们用来描述任何社会中权力运作的术语。无论何时，只要人类聚集在一起做任何事情，权力的分配总是极不均衡的。在公司、医院、宗教、政府机构等等，高层拥有巨大的权力，底层民众几乎没有权力，而中间阶层则拥有一定的权力。那么，一个普通劳动者如何获得或失去权力呢？无论我们如何努力消除不平等，运用各种平等主义理论，人类社会的权力结构本质上都是金字塔式的。换句话说，这就是政治。

Even when writing about a household, question its politics, for like any other social structure, a family is political. Is it a patriarchal home where Dad has the clout, but when he leaves the house, it transfers to Mom, then when she’s out, to the oldest child? Or is it a matriarchal home, where Mom runs things? Or a contemporary family in which the kid is tyrannizing his parents?

即使是描写一个家庭，也要质疑其政治内涵，因为像其他任何社会结构一样，家庭也具有政治性。这是一个父权制家庭吗？父亲拥有权力，但当他离开家时，权力就转移到母亲身上；母亲不在家时，权力又转移到最大的孩子身上。或者这是一个母权制家庭，母亲主宰一切？又或者是一个孩子凌驾于父母之上的当代家庭？

Love relationships are political. An old Gypsy expression goes: “He who confesses first loses.” The first person to say “I love you” has lost because the other, upon hearing it, immediately smiles a knowing smile, realizing that he’s the one loved, so he now controls the relationship. If you’re lucky, those three little words will be said in unison over candlelight. Or, if very, very lucky, they won’t need to be said… they’ll be done.

爱情关系是一种政治。一句古老的吉普赛谚语说：“先表白的人输了。” 第一个说“我爱你”的人已经输了，因为对方听到这句话后，会立刻露出心照不宣的微笑，意识到自己才是被爱的那个人，于是他便掌控了这段关系。如果你足够幸运，这三个字会在烛光下齐声说出。或者，如果你非常非常幸运，它们甚至无需说出口……一切都已成定局。

What are the rituals of my world? In all corners of the world life is bound up in ritual. This is a ritual, is it not? I’ve written a book and you’re reading it. In another time and place we might sit under a tree or take a walk, like Socrates and his students. We create a ritual for every activity, not only for public ceremony but for our very private rites. Heaven help the person who rearranges my organization of toiletries around the bathroom basin.

我的世界里有哪些仪式？在世界各地，生活都与仪式息息相关。这本身就是一种仪式，不是吗？我写了一本书，而你正在读它。在另一个时空，我们或许会像苏格拉底和他的学生那样，坐在树下或散步。我们为每项活动都创造了仪式，不仅是公共仪式，也包括我们极其私密的仪式。谁要是敢动我浴室洗手盆周围摆放的洗漱用品，老天保佑他。

How do your characters take meals? Eating is a different ritual everywhere in the world. Americans, for example, according to a recent survey, now eat 75 percent of all their meals in restaurants. If your characters eat at home, is it an old-fashioned family that dresses for dinner at a certain hour, or a contemporary one that feeds from an open refrigerator?

你的角色是如何用餐的？世界各地的饮食习惯都不尽相同。例如，根据最近的一项调查，美国人现在75%的餐食都在餐馆解决。如果你的角色在家用餐，他们是会在特定时间盛装打扮去吃晚饭的传统家庭，还是会直接从敞开的冰箱里拿食物的现代家庭呢？

What are the values in my world? What do my characters consider good? Evil? What do they see as right? Wrong? What are my society’s laws? Realize that good/evil, right/wrong, and legal/illegal don’t necessarily have anything to do with one another. What do my characters believe is worth living for? Foolish to pursue? What would they give their lives for?

我的世界里有哪些价值观？我的角色认为什么是善？什么是恶？他们认为什么是对的？什么是错的？我的社会有哪些法律？要知道，善恶、对错、合法与非法之间并不一定存在关联。我的角色认为什么值得为之而活？什么又是愚蠢的？他们会为了什么而献出生命？

What is the genre or combination of genres? With what conventions? As with setting, genres surround the writer with creative limitations that must be kept or brilliantly altered.

这部作品属于哪种体裁，或者说是几种体裁的组合？它遵循哪些惯例？就像故事背景一样，体裁也给作家带来了创作上的限制，作家必须遵守这些限制，或者巧妙地加以改造。

What are the biographies of my characters? From the day they were born to the opening scene, how has life shaped them?

我的角色们都有怎样的人生经历？从他们出生到影片开场，生活是如何塑造他们的？

What is the Backstory? This is an oft-misunderstood term. It doesn’t mean life history or biography. Backstory is the set of significant events that occurred in the characters’ past that the writer can use to build his story’s progressions. Exactly how we use Backstory to tell story will be discussed later, but for the moment note that we do not bring characters out of a void. We landscape character biographies, planting them with events that become a garden we’ll harvest again and again.

什么是背景故事？这是一个经常被误解的术语。它并非指人物的生平或传记。背景故事指的是角色过去经历中发生的一系列重要事件，作者可以利用这些事件来构建故事的发展脉络。我们将在后面详细讨论如何运用背景故事来讲述故事，但现在需要注意的是，我们并非凭空创造角色。我们为角色的人生经历增添色彩，播撒各种事件的种子，最终形成一座可以反复采摘的花园。

What is my cast design? Nothing in a work of art is there by accident. Ideas may come spontaneously, but we must weave them consciously and creatively into the whole. We cannot allow any character who comes to mind to stumble into the story and play a part. Each role must fit a purpose, and the first principle of cast design is polarization. Between the various roles we devise a network of contrasting or contradictory attitudes.

我的演员阵容设计是什么？艺术作品中的任何元素都不是偶然产生的。灵感或许会自然而然地涌现，但我们必须有意识地、创造性地将它们融入整体。我们不能让任何一个脑海中浮现的角色随意闯入故事并扮演任何角色。每个角色都必须服务于特定的目的，而演员阵容设计的首要原则就是两极分化。我们通过构建不同角色之间对比鲜明或相互矛盾的态度网络，来塑造角色形象。

If the ideal cast sat down for dinner and something happened, whether as trivial as spilled wine or as important as a divorce announcement, from each and every character would come a separate and distinctively different reaction. No two would react the same because no two share the same attitude toward anything. Each is an individual with a character-specific view of life, and the disparate reaction of each contrasts with all others.

如果一群理想的演员围坐在一起吃晚餐，这时发生了一件事，无论是像洒了酒这样的小事，还是像宣布离婚这样的大事，每个角色都会做出截然不同的反应。没有两个人会做出相同的反应，因为没有人会对任何事持有相同的态度。每个人都是一个独立的个体，有着各自独特的人生观，而每个人的反应都与其他所有人的反应形成了鲜明的对比。

If two characters in your cast share the same attitude and react in kind to whatever occurs, you must either collapse the two into one, or expel one from the story. When characters react the same, you minimize opportunities for conflict. Instead, the writer’s strategy must be to maximize these opportunities.

如果两个角色态度相同，对任何事情的反应都如出一辙，那么你必须要么将他们合并为一个，要么将其中一个从故事中剔除。当角色反应一致时，冲突的机会就会大大减少。因此，编剧的策略应该是尽可能地创造和利用这些机会。

Imagine this cast: father, mother, daughter, and a son named Jeffrey. This family lives in Iowa. As they sit down for dinner, Jeffrey turns to them and says: “Mom, Dad, Sis, I’ve come to a big decision. I have an airline ticket and tomorrow I’m leaving for Hollywood to pursue a career as an art director in the movies.” And all three respond: “Oh, what a wonderful idea! Isn’t that great? Jeff’s going off to Hollywood!” And they toast him with their glasses of milk.

想象一下这样的家庭：父亲、母亲、女儿，还有一个名叫杰弗里的儿子。他们住在爱荷华州。一家人坐下来吃晚饭时，杰弗里转过头对他们说：“爸爸妈妈，妹妹，我做了一个重大决定。我买了机票，明天就要去好莱坞，追寻我作为电影艺术指导的梦想。” 三个人异口同声地说：“哦，真是个好主意！太棒了！杰夫要去好莱坞了！” 他们举起手中的牛奶杯，为他干杯。

CUT TO: Jeff’s room, where they help him pack while admiring his pictures on the wall, reflecting nostalgically on his days in art school, complimenting his talent, predicting success.

镜头切换到：杰夫的房间，大家一边帮他收拾行李，一边欣赏墙上他的照片，怀念着他在艺术学校的日子，称赞他的才华，预言他会成功。

CUT TO: The airport as the family puts Jeff on the plane, tears in their eyes, embracing him: “Write when you get work, Jeff.”

镜头切换到：机场，一家人含着泪把杰夫送上飞机，拥抱着他：“杰夫，等你找到工作就写东西吧。”

Suppose, instead, Jeffrey sits down for dinner, delivers his declaration, and suddenly Dad’s fist POUNDS the table: “What the hell are you talking about, Jeff? You’re not going off to Hollyweird to become some art director… whatever an art director is. No, you’re staying right here in Davenport. Because, Jeff, as you know, I have never done anything for myself. Not in my entire life. It’s all for you, Jeff, for you! Granted, I’m the king of plumbing supplies in Iowa… but someday, son, you’ll be emperor of plumbing supplies all over the Midwest and I won’t hear another word of this nonsense. End of discussion.”

假设杰弗里坐下来吃晚饭，发表了一番宣言，突然，爸爸一拳砸在桌子上：“杰夫，你到底在胡说什么？你休想去好莱坞当什么艺术总监……不管艺术总监是干什么的。不，你就待在达文波特。因为，杰夫，你知道的，我这辈子从来没为自己做过任何事。从来没有。一切都是为了你，杰夫，都是为了你！没错，我是爱荷华州的管道用品大王……但总有一天，儿子，你会成为整个中西部地区的管道用品皇帝，到时候我别想再听你胡说八道。就此打住。”

CUT TO: Jeff sulking in his room. His mother slips in whispering: “Don’t you listen to him. Go off to Hollywood, become an art director… whatever that is. Do they win Oscars for that, Jeff?” “Yes, Mom, they do,” Jeff says. “Good! Go off to Hollywood and win me an Oscar and prove that bastard wrong. And you can do it, Jeff. Because you’ve got talent. I know you’ve got talent. You got that from my side of the family. I used to have talent too, but I gave it all up when I married your father, and I’ve regretted it ever since. For God’s sake, Jeff, don’t sit here in Davenport. Hell, this town was named after a sofa. No, go off to Hollywood and make me proud.”

镜头切换：杰夫独自在房间里生闷气。他妈妈悄悄走进来，低声说：“别听他的。去好莱坞，当个艺术指导……不管那是什么。杰夫，他们做这个能拿奥斯卡吗？”“能，妈，”杰夫说。“好！去好莱坞，给我拿个奥斯卡，证明那个混蛋错了。你能做到，杰夫。因为你有天赋。我知道你有天赋。这是遗传自我家的。我以前也很有天赋，但嫁给你爸爸之后就放弃了，我一直后悔。看在上帝的份上，杰夫，别待在达文波特了。见鬼，这镇子的名字都跟沙发有关。不，去好莱坞，让我为你骄傲。”

CUT TO: Jeff packing. His sister comes in, shocked, “Jeff! What are you doing? Packing? Leaving me alone? With those two? You know how they are. They’ll eat me alive. If you go off to Hollywood, I’ll end up in the plumbing supply business!” Pulling his stuff out of the suitcase: “If you wanna be an artist, you can be an artist anywhere. A sunset’s a sunset. A landscape’s a landscape. What the hell difference does it make? And someday you’ll have success. I know you will. I’ve seen paintings just like yours… in Sears. Don’t leave, Jeff! I’ll die!”

镜头切换：杰夫正在收拾行李。他妹妹冲进来，震惊地说：“杰夫！你在干什么？收拾行李？把我一个人留下？跟那两个人？你知道他们是什么样的人。他们会把我生吞活剥的。你要是去了好莱坞，我就只能去卖水暖器材了！” 他一边从箱子里拿出东西一边说：“如果你想当艺术家，哪里都能当艺术家。日落就是日落，风景就是风景。这有什么区别？总有一天你会成功的。我知道你会的。我在西尔斯百货见过跟你画的一样的画……别走，杰夫！我会死的！”

Whether or not Jeff goes off to Hollywood, the polarized cast gives the writer something we all desperately need: scenes.

无论杰夫是否前往好莱坞发展，两极分化的演员阵容都为编剧提供了我们都迫切需要的东西：场景。

AUTHORSHIP

作者身份

When research of setting reaches the saturation point, something miraculous happens. Your story takes on a unique atmosphere, a personality that sets it apart from every other story ever told, no matter how many millions there have been through time. It’s an amazing phenomenon: Human beings have told one another stories since they sat around the fire in caves, and every time the storyteller uses the art in its fullest, his story, like a portrait by a master painter, becomes one of a kind.

当对故事背景的考察达到饱和点时，奇迹就会发生。你的故事会散发出一种独特的氛围，一种与众不同的个性，使其与历史上无数其他故事都截然不同。这是一种奇妙的现象：自从人类在山洞里围坐在篝火旁讲述故事以来，就一直如此。每当讲故事的人将这种艺术形式发挥到极致，他的故事就如同大师的画作一般，成为独一无二的珍品。

Like the stories you’re striving to tell, you want to be one of a kind, recognized and respected as an original. In your quest, consider these three words: “author,” “authority,” “authenticity.”

就像你努力讲述的故事一样，你渴望独一无二，被认可并尊重为原创者。在你的追求过程中，请思考这三个词：“作者”、“权威”、“真实性”。

First, “author.” “Author” is a title we easily give novelists and playwrights, rarely screenwriters. But in the strict sense of “originator,” the screenwriter, as creator of setting, characters, and story, is an author. For the test of authorship is knowledge. A true author, no matter the medium, is an artist with godlike knowledge of his subject, and the proof of his authorship is that his pages smack of authority. What a rare pleasure it is to open a screenplay and immediately surrender to the work, giving over emotion and concentration because there is something ineffable between and under the lines that says: “This writer knows. I’m in the hands of an authority.” And the effect of writing with authority is authenticity.

首先是“作者”。我们常常用“作者”这个头衔来称呼小说家和剧作家，却很少用来称呼编剧。但严格来说，从“创作者”的角度来看，编剧作为场景、人物和故事的创造者，也是一位作者。因为检验作者身份的标准在于知识。一位真正的作者，无论创作媒介如何，都是一位对其主题拥有渊博知识的艺术家，而他作品中流露出的权威性，正是其作者身份的证明。打开一个剧本，立刻沉浸其中，全神贯注，因为字里行间蕴含着某种难以言喻的力量，仿佛在说：“这位作者很懂行。我仿佛置身于一位权威的掌控之中。”这是一种多么难得的享受啊！而这种权威的写作方式所带来的效果，便是真实感。

Two principles control the emotional involvement of an audience. First, empathy: identification with the protagonist that draws us into the story, vicariously rooting for our own desires in life. Second, authenticity: We must believe , or as Samuel Taylor Coleridge suggested, we must willingly suspend our disbelief. Once involved, the writer must keep us involved to FADE OUT. To do so, he must convince us that the world of his story is authentic. We know that storytelling is a ritual surrounding a metaphor for life. To enjoy this ceremony in the dark we react to stories as if they’re real. We suspend our cynicism and believe in the tale as long as we find it authentic. The moment it lacks credibility, empathy dissolves and we feel nothing.

有两个原则控制着观众的情感投入。首先是共情：与主人公产生认同感，将我们带入故事，让我们感同身受地为自己的人生愿望而努力。其次是真实性：我们必须相信，或者如塞缪尔·泰勒·柯勒律治所言，我们必须心甘情愿地暂时放下怀疑。一旦投入其中，作者就必须让我们保持这种状态，直到故事淡出。为此，他必须让我们相信他所讲述的世界是真实的。我们知道，讲故事是一种围绕人生隐喻的仪式。为了享受这种在黑暗中进行的仪式，我们会像对待真实故事一样对待它们。只要我们认为故事真实可信，我们就会暂时放下怀疑，相信它。一旦故事缺乏可信度，共情就会消失，我们便会麻木不仁。

Authenticity, however, does not mean actuality. Giving a story a contemporary milieu is no guarantee of authenticity; authenticity means an internally consistent world, true to itself in scope, depth, and detail. As Aristotle tells us: “For the purposes of [story] a convincing impossibility is preferable to an unconvincing possibility.” We can all list films that had us moaning: “I don’t buy it. People aren’t like that. Makes no sense. That’s not how things happen.”

然而，真实性并不等同于现实性。将故事置于当代背景并不能保证其真实性；真实性指的是一个内部逻辑自洽的世界，在广度、深度和细节上都忠于自身。正如亚里士多德所说：“就故事而言，令人信服的不可能比不令人信服的可能性更可取。”我们都能列举出一些让我们叹息的电影：“我不信。人不是这样的。这说不通。事情根本不是这样的。”
