“类别”指的是从物质世界中提取的、足够宽泛以容纳足够多样性的主题。例如，自然的一个维度——动物、季节、光与暗——或者人类文化的一个维度——建筑、机器、艺术。这个类别必须重复出现，因为一两个孤立的符号几乎不起作用。但是，有组织的影像重复的力量是巨大的，因为多样性和重复性会将影像系统推向观众潜意识的深处。然而，最重要的是，电影的诗学必须以近乎隐形的方式处理，并且不能被观众有意识地察觉。

An Image System is created one of two ways, via External or Internal Imagery. External Imagery takes a category that outside the film already has a symbolic meaning and brings it in to mean the same thing in the film it means outside the film: for example, to use the national flag—a symbol of patriotism and love of country—to mean patriotism, love of country. In ROCKY IV, for example, after Rocky defeats the Russian boxer, he wraps himself in a massive American flag. Or to use a crucifix, a symbol of love of God and religious feelings, to mean love of God, religious feelings; a spider’s web to mean entrapment; a teardrop to mean sadness. External Imagery, I must point out, is the hallmark of the student film.

影像系统的构建方式有两种：外部意象和内部意象。外部意象是指将电影之外已具有象征意义的事物引入电影，使其在电影中表达与电影之外相同的含义：例如，使用国旗——爱国主义和爱国情怀的象征——来表达爱国主义和爱国情怀。例如，在《洛奇4》中，洛奇击败俄罗斯拳击手后，用一面巨大的美国国旗裹住了自己。又如，使用十字架——爱上帝和宗教情感的象征——来表达爱上帝和宗教情感；使用蜘蛛网来表达困住；使用泪滴来表达悲伤。我必须指出，外部意象是学生电影的标志性特征。

Internal Imagery takes a category that outside the film may or may not have a symbolic meaning attached but brings it into the film to give it an entirely new meaning appropriate to this film and this film alone.

内部意象是指将电影之外可能具有也可能不具有象征意义的类别引入电影中，赋予其只适用于这部电影的全新意义。

LES DIABOLIQUE: In 1955 director/screenwriter Henri-Georges Clouzot adapted Pierre Boileau’s novel, Celle Qui N’etait Pas to the screen. In it Christina (Vera Clouzot) is an attractive young woman but very shy, quiet, and sensitive. She has suffered from a heart condition since childhood and is never in the best of health. Years before she inherited an impressive estate in the suburbs of Paris that has been turned into an exclusive boarding school. She runs this school with her husband, Michel (Paul Meurisse), a sadistic, abusive, malignant bastard who delights in treating his wife like dirt. He’s having an affair with one of the school’s teachers, Nicole (Simone Signoret), and he’s as vicious and cruel to his mistress as he is to his wife.

《恶魔》：1955年，导演兼编剧亨利-乔治·克鲁佐将皮埃尔·布瓦洛的小说《没有她的人》改编成了电影。影片中，克里斯蒂娜（薇拉·克鲁佐饰）是一位年轻貌美的女子，但她非常害羞、安静且敏感。她自幼患有心脏病，身体一直不太好。多年前，她继承了巴黎郊区一座气派的庄园，并将其改建成了一所贵族寄宿学校。她与丈夫米歇尔（保罗·默里斯饰）共同经营这所学校。米歇尔是一个虐待成性、心狠手辣的混蛋，他以虐待妻子为乐。他与学校的一位老师妮可（西蒙·西涅莱饰）有染，他对情妇的残忍和恶毒丝毫不亚于对待妻子。

Everybody knows about this affair. In fact, the two women have become best friends, both suffering under the heel of this brute. Early in the film they decide that the only way out of their problem is to kill him.

所有人都知道这件事。事实上，这两个女人成了最好的朋友，她们都饱受这个恶棍的欺凌。影片一开始，她们就认定摆脱困境的唯一办法就是杀了他。

One night they lure Michel to an apartment in a village well away from the school where they’ve secretly filled a bathtub full of water. He comes in, dressed in his three-piece suit, and arrogantly taunts and insults his two women while they get him as drunk as they possibly can, then try to drown him in the bathtub. But he’s not that drunk and it’s a hell of a struggle. The terror nearly kills the poor wife, but Nicole rushes into the living room and grabs a ceramic statue of a panther from the coffee table. She loads this heavy thing on the man’s chest. Between the weight of the statue and her own strength she manages to hold him down under the water long enough to drown him.

一天晚上，她们把米歇尔骗到离学校很远的一个村庄里的公寓，偷偷地在浴缸里灌满了水。他穿着三件套西装进来，傲慢地嘲讽侮辱她的两个女人，而她们则想方设法把他灌醉，然后试图把他淹死在浴缸里。但他并没有醉得很厉害，挣扎得非常艰难。可怜的妻子几乎被吓死了，但妮可冲进客厅，从茶几上抓起一尊陶瓷豹子雕像。她把这沉重的雕像压在男人的胸口。凭借雕像的重量和她自己的力量，她成功地把他按在水下，直到他溺水身亡。

The women wrap the body in a tarp, hide it in the back of a pickup truck, and sneak back to the campus in the middle of the night. The school’s swimming pool hasn’t been used all winter; an inch of algae covers the water. The women dump the body in and it submerges out of sight. They quickly retire and wait for the next day when the body will float up and be discovered. But the next day comes and goes and the body does not float up. Days go by and the body will not float up.

女人们用防水布裹住尸体，藏在皮卡车的后车厢里，半夜偷偷溜回校园。学校的游泳池整个冬天都没用过，水面上长了一英寸厚的藻类。她们把尸体扔进水里，尸体沉入水底，消失不见。她们匆匆回家，等着第二天尸体浮上来被发现。可是第二天过去了，尸体却没有浮上来。日子一天天过去，尸体依然没有浮上来。

Finally, Nicole accidentally on purpose drops her car keys in the pool and asks one of the older students to retrieve them. The kid dives down under the scum and searches and searches and searches. He comes up, gulps some air, then goes down again and searches and searches and searches. He comes up to gulp air, then goes down a third time and searches and searches and searches. At last he surfaces… with the car keys.

最后，妮可故意把车钥匙掉进泳池里，然后让一个高年级的学生去捡。那孩子潜入水底，在浮渣下不停地搜寻。他浮出水面，喘了口气，然后又潜下去，继续搜寻。他再次浮出水面喘气，然后第三次潜入水中，继续搜寻。最后，他终于浮出水面……找到了车钥匙。

The women then decide it’s time to clean the swimming pool. They order the pool drained and stand at its edge, watching as the scum goes down and down and down and down… to the drain. But there is no body. That afternoon a dry cleaner’s van drives out from Paris to deliver the cleaned and pressed suit that the man died in. The women rush into Paris to the cleaners where they find a receipt, and on it is the address of a boardinghouse. They head there and talk to a concierge who says, “Yes, yes, there was a man living here but… he moved this morning.”

于是，女人们决定清理游泳池。她们叫人把水抽干，站在池边，看着水垢一滴一滴地沉入排水沟。但池子里没有尸体。当天下午，一辆干洗店的货车从巴黎开来，送来了那名男子死时穿的干净熨烫好的西装。女人们急忙赶到巴黎的干洗店，在那里找到了一张收据，上面写着一家旅馆的地址。她们前往旅馆，找到一位门房，门房说：“是的，是的，这里以前住着一个男人，但是……他今天早上搬走了。”

They go back to the school and even more bizarre things happen: Michel appears and disappears in the windows of the school. When they look at the senior class graduation photo, there he is standing behind the students, slightly out of focus. They can’t imagine what’s going on. Is he a ghost? Did he somehow survive the drowning and he’s doing this to us? Did someone else find the body? Are they doing this?

他们回到学校，更诡异的事情发生了：米歇尔的身影在学校的窗户里忽隐忽现。当他们看毕业照时，发现他站在学生身后，只是画面有些模糊。他们百思不得其解。他是鬼魂吗？他溺水后奇迹般地活了下来，然后故意捉弄我们？还是有人发现了尸体？是他们干的？

Summer vacation comes and all the students and teachers leave. Then Nicole herself departs. She packs her bags, saying she can’t take this anymore, abandoning the poor wife alone.

暑假来临，师生们都离开了。妮可自己也走了。她收拾好行李，说她再也受不了了，留下可怜的妻子孤零零一个人。

That evening Christina can’t sleep; she sits up in bed, wide awake, her heart pounding. Suddenly in the dead of night she hears the sound of typing coming from her husband’s office. She slowly gets up and edges down a long corridor, hand on her heart, but just as she touches the office doorknob, the typing stops.

那天晚上，克里斯蒂娜辗转反侧，难以入眠；她坐起身来，心跳如擂鼓，完全清醒。突然，在夜深人静之时，她听到丈夫办公室里传来打字的声音。她缓缓起身，沿着长长的走廊踱步而去，手抚着胸口，但就在她触碰到办公室门把手的那一刻，打字声戛然而止。

She eases open the door and there, alongside the typewriter, are her husband’s gloves… like two huge hands. Then she hears the most terrifying sound imaginable: dripping water. Now she heads toward the bathroom off the office, her heart raging. She creaks open the bathroom door and there he is—still in his three-piece suit, submerged in a bathtub full of water, the faucet dripping.

她轻轻推开门，只见打字机旁边放着她丈夫的手套……像两只巨大的手。接着，她听到了最恐怖的声音：滴水声。她心跳加速，朝办公室旁边的浴室走去。她吱呀一声推开浴室门，只见他——还穿着三件套西装，泡在装满水的浴缸里，水龙头滴着水。

The body sits up, water cascades off. Its eyes open but there are no eyeballs. Hands reach out for her, she grabs her chest, has a fatal heart attack, and drops dead on the floor. Michel reaches under his eyelids and removes white plastic inserts. Nicole jumps out of a closet. They embrace and whisper, “We did it!”

尸体坐了起来，水流倾泻而下。它睁开眼睛，却不见眼球。有人伸手去抓她，她捂住胸口，突发心脏病，倒在地上死去。米歇尔伸手到眼睑下，取出白色的塑料片。妮可从衣橱里跳了出来。他们拥抱在一起，低声说：“我们成功了！”

The opening titles of LES DIABOLIQUE look as if they’re over an abstract painting of grays and blacks. But suddenly, as titles end, a truck tire splashes from bottom to top of the screen and we realize we’ve been looking at the top angle view of a mud puddle. The camera comes up on a rainy landscape. From this first moment on, Image System “water” is continually and subliminally repeated. It’s always drizzly and foggy. Condensation on windows runs in little drops to the sills. At dinner they eat fish. Characters drink wine and tea while Christina sips her heart medicine. When the teachers discuss summer vacation, they talk of going to the South of France to “take the waters.” Swimming pool, bathtubs… it’s one of the dampest films ever made.

《恶魔》的片头字幕仿佛叠加在一幅灰黑相间的抽象画作之上。然而，字幕结束后，突然一个卡车轮胎溅起的水花从屏幕底部冲上顶部，我们这才意识到，刚才看到的其实是一个泥坑的俯视图。镜头缓缓拉近，展现出一片雨中的景象。从这第一个瞬间开始，“水”这个意象便不断被潜移默化地重复出现。这里总是阴雨绵绵，雾气弥漫。窗户上的水汽凝结成小水滴，顺着窗台流淌。晚餐时，他们吃的是鱼。角色们喝着葡萄酒和茶，克里斯蒂娜则在啜饮着她的心脏病药物。老师们讨论暑假计划时，提到了去法国南部“泡温泉”。游泳池、浴缸……这绝对是有史以来最潮湿的电影之一。

Outside this film water is a universal symbol of all things positive: sanctification, purification, the feminine—archetype for life itself. But Clouzot reverses these values until water takes on the power of death, terror, and evil, and the sound of a dripping faucet brings the audience up out of its seats.

在这部电影之外，水是象征一切美好事物的普世符号：神圣、净化、女性特质——生命本身的原型。但克鲁佐颠覆了这些价值，使水拥有了死亡、恐惧和邪恶的力量，滴水的水龙头声甚至能让观众从座位上站起来。

CASABLANCA weaves three Image Systems. Its primary motifs create a sense of imprisonment as the city of Casablanca becomes a virtual penitentiary. Characters whisper their “escape” plans as if the police were prison guards. The beacon on the airport tower moves through the streets like a searchlight scanning a prison compound, while window blinds, room dividers, stair railings, even the leaves of potted palms create shadows like the bars of prison cells.

《卡萨布兰卡》巧妙地融合了三个意象系统。其主要意象营造出一种囚禁感，卡萨布兰卡这座城市仿佛变成了一座监狱。片中人物低声密谋“越狱”计划，仿佛警察就是狱卒。机场塔台上的灯塔如同探照灯般在街道上移动，扫视着监狱大院；而百叶窗、房间隔断、楼梯扶手，甚至盆栽棕榈树的叶子，都投下如同监狱牢房铁栏杆般的阴影。

The second system builds a progression from the particular to the archetypal. Casablanca starts as a refugee center but becomes a mini-United Nations filled with not only Arab and European faces but Asian and African ones as well. Rick and his friend Sam are the only Americans we meet. Repeated images, including dialogue in which characters speak to Rick as if he were a country, associate Rick to America until he comes to symbolize America itself and Casablanca the world. Like the United States in 1941 Rick is steadfastly neutral, wanting no part in yet another World War. His conversion to the fight subliminally congratulates America for finally taking sides against tyranny.

第二个体系构建了一个从具体到原型的渐进过程。《卡萨布兰卡》最初是一个难民营，后来发展成一个小型联合国，其中不仅有阿拉伯人和欧洲人，还有亚洲人和非洲人。里克和他的朋友萨姆是我们遇到的仅有的美国人。反复出现的意象，包括角色们将里克视为一个国家进行对话的场景，将里克与美国联系起来，最终里克成为美国的象征，而卡萨布兰卡则象征着世界。如同1941年的美国一样，里克坚定地保持中立，不愿卷入另一场世界大战。他最终加入战争，潜意识里是在祝贺美国终于站出来反对暴政。

The third system is one of linking and separating. A number of images and compositions within the frame are used to link Rick and Ilsa, making the subliminal point that although these two are apart, they belong together. The counterpoint to this is a series of images and compositional designs that separate Ilsa from Laszlo, giving the opposite impression that although these two are together, they belong apart.

第三种系统是连接与分离。画面中运用了一系列图像和构图来连接里克和伊尔莎，潜移默化地暗示他们虽身处异地，却又彼此相连。与之形成对比的是，一系列图像和构图设计将伊尔莎与拉斯洛分隔开来，给人以相反的印象：他们虽身处异地，却又彼此疏离。

THROUGH A GLASS DARKLY is a multiplot film with six story lines—three positive climaxes devoted to the father, three negative endings to his daughter—in a point/counterpoint design that interweaves no fewer than four Image Systems. The father’s stories are marked by open spaces, light, intellect, and verbal communication; the daughter’s conflicts are expressed in closed spaces, darkness, animal images, and sexuality.

《透过黑暗的玻璃》是一部多线叙事电影，由六条故事线构成——三条以父亲为中心的正面高潮，三条以女儿为中心的负面结局——采用正反对比的结构，交织了不少于四种意象系统。父亲的故事以开阔的空间、光线、智慧和语言交流为特征；女儿的冲突则通过封闭的空间、黑暗、动物意象和性来表达。

CHINATOWN also employs four systems, two of External Imagery, two of Internal Imagery. The primary internalized system is motifs of “blind seeing” or seeing falsely: Windows; rearview mirrors; eyeglasses, and particularly broken spectacles; cameras; binoculars; eyes themselves, and even the open, unseeing eyes of the dead, all gather tremendous forces to suggest that if we are looking for evil out in the world, we’re looking in the wrong direction. It is in here. In us. As Mao Tse-tung once said, “History is the symptom, we are the disease.”

《唐人街》也运用了四种意象系统，两种外部意象，两种内部意象。主要的内部意象系统是“盲目观看”或“虚假观看”的主题：窗户；后视镜；眼镜，尤其是破损的眼镜；相机；望远镜；眼睛本身，甚至死者睁着却看不见的眼睛，所有这些都汇聚成一股强大的力量，暗示着如果我们向外寻找邪恶，那就找错了方向。邪恶就在我们自身之内。正如毛泽东所说：“历史是症状，我们才是病根。”

The second internalized system takes political corruption and turns it into social cement. False contracts, subverted laws, and acts of corruption become that which hold society together and create “progress.” Two systems of External Imagery, water versus drought and sexual cruelty versus sexual love have conventional connotations but are used with a sharp-edged effectiveness.

第二套内在系统将政治腐败转化为社会凝聚力。虚假契约、被颠覆的法律和腐败行为成为维系社会、创造“进步”的纽带。两种外部意象——水与旱、性虐待与性爱——虽然具有传统的含义，却被巧妙地运用，产生了尖锐而有效的效果。

When ALIEN was released Time magazine ran a ten-page article with stills and drawings asking the question: Has Hollywood gone too far? For this film incorporates a highly erotic Image System and contains three vivid “rape” scenes.

《异形》上映时，《时代》杂志刊登了一篇长达十页的文章，配以剧照和插图，提出了这样一个问题：好莱坞是否做得太过火了？因为这部电影采用了高度情色的图像系统，并包含三个生动的“强奸”场景。

When Gail Anne Hurd and James Cameron made the sequel, ALIENS, they not only switched genres from Horror to Action/Adventure , they reinvented the Image System to motherhood as Ripley becomes the surrogate mother of the child Newt (Carrie Henn), who in turn is the surrogate mother of her broken doll. The two are up against the most terrifying “mother” in the universe, the gigantic monster queen who lays her eggs in a womblike nest. In dialogue, Ripley remarks, “The monsters make you pregnant.”

盖尔·安妮·赫德和詹姆斯·卡梅隆在拍摄续集《异形2》时，不仅将类型从恐怖片转向动作/冒险片，还重塑了母性形象：雷普利成为纽特（凯莉·亨饰）的代孕母亲，而纽特又成为她破碎玩偶的代孕母亲。两人要对抗的是宇宙中最恐怖的“母亲”——巨型怪物女王，她将卵产在类似子宫的巢穴中。雷普利在片中说道：“怪物会让你怀孕。”

AFTER HOURS works on only one internalized refrain but with a rich variety: Art. But not as the ornament of life. Rather, art as a weapon. The art and artists of Manhattan’s Soho district constantly assault the protagonist, Paul (Griffin Dunne), until he’s encapsulated inside a work of art and stolen by Cheech and Chong.

《下班后》的核心主题只有一个，但却以丰富的形式呈现出来：艺术。但艺术并非生活的装饰，而是一种武器。曼哈顿苏豪区的艺术和艺术家们不断地侵扰着主人公保罗（格里芬·邓恩饰），直到他被包裹在一件艺术品中，并被奇奇和冲偷走。

Going back through the decades, Hitchcock’s Thrillers combine images of religiosity with sexuality, while John Ford’s Westerns counterpoint wilderness with civilization. In fact, traveling back through the centuries we realize that Image Systems are as old as story itself. Homer invented beautiful motifs for his epics, as did Aeschylus, Sophocles, and Euripides for their plays. Shakespeare submerged a unique Image System into each of his works, as did Melville, Poe, Tolstoy, Dickens, Orwell, Hemingway, Ibsen, Chekhov, Shaw, Beckett—all great novelists and playwrights have embraced this principle.

回顾几十年，希区柯克的惊悚片将宗教意象与性爱融合在一起，而约翰·福特的西部片则将荒野与文明形成鲜明对比。事实上，追溯历史长河，我们会发现意象系统与故事本身一样古老。荷马为他的史诗创造了优美的主题，埃斯库罗斯、索福克勒斯和欧里庇得斯也为他们的戏剧创作了类似的意象。莎士比亚在他的每一部作品中都融入了独特的意象系统，梅尔维尔、爱伦·坡、托尔斯泰、狄更斯、奥威尔、海明威、易卜生、契诃夫、萧伯纳、贝克特——所有伟大的小说家和剧作家都遵循了这一原则。

And who, after all, invented screenwriting? Novelists and playwrights who came to the cradles of our art in Hollywood, London, Paris, Berlin, Tokyo, and Moscow to write the scenarios of silent films. Film’s first major directors, such as D. W. Griffith, Eisenstein, and Murnau, did their apprenticeship in the theatre; they too realized that, like a fine play, a film can be taken to the sublime by the repetition of a subliminal poetics.

那么，究竟是谁发明了剧本创作呢？是那些来到好莱坞、伦敦、巴黎、柏林、东京和莫斯科——电影艺术的摇篮——的小说家和剧作家，他们为默片创作剧本。电影史上第一批重要的导演，如D·W·格里菲斯、爱森斯坦和穆瑙，都曾在剧院接受过训练；他们也意识到，就像一部优秀的戏剧一样，电影可以通过对潜意识诗学的重复运用，达到崇高的境界。

And an Image System must be subliminal. The audience is not to be aware of it. Years ago as I watched Buñuel’s VIRIDIANA, I noticed that Buñuel had introduced an Image System of rope: A child jump ropes, a rich man hangs himself with a rope, a poor man uses rope as a belt. About the fifth time a piece of rope came on the screen the audience shouted in unison, “Symbol!”

而且，图像系统必须是潜意识的。观众不应该意识到它的存在。多年前，我观看布努埃尔的《维莉蒂安娜》时，注意到布努埃尔引入了一个绳索的图像系统：一个孩子在跳绳，一个富人用绳子上吊，一个穷人用绳子做腰带。当绳子第五次出现在银幕上时，观众齐声喊道：“象征！”

Symbolism is powerful, more powerful than most realize, as long as it bypasses the conscious mind and slips into the unconscious. As it does while we dream. The use of symbolism follows the same principle as scoring a film. Sound doesn’t need cognition, so music can deeply affect us when we’re unconscious of it. In the same way, symbols touch us and move us— as long as we don’t recognize them as symbolic. Awareness of a symbol turns it into a neutral, intellectual curiosity, powerless and virtually meaningless.

象征主义的力量强大，远超大多数人的想象，只要它能绕过意识，悄然潜入潜意识，就像我们在做梦时那样。象征主义的运用与电影配乐遵循着相同的原则。声音无需认知，因此音乐可以在我们无意识的情况下深深地影响我们。同样，只要我们不意识到符号的象征意义，符号也能触动我们，感动我们。一旦意识到符号的象征意义，它就变成了一种中性的、纯粹的、知识性的好奇物，失去了力量，几乎毫无意义。

Why, then, do so many contemporary writer/directors label their symbols? The hamhanded treatment of “symbolic” images in the remake of CAPE FEAR, BRAM STOKER’S DRACULA, and THE PIANO, to name three of the more barefaced examples. I can think of two likely reasons: First, to flatter the elite audience of self-perceived intellectuals that watches at a safe, unemotional distance while collecting ammunition for the postfilm ritual of cafe criticism. Second, to influence, if not control, critics and the reviews they write. Declamatory symbolism requires no genius, just egotism ignited by misreadings of Jung and Derrida. It is a vanity that demeans and corrupts the art.

那么，为什么这么多当代编剧/导演要给他们的作品中的符号贴上标签呢？《恐怖角》、《吸血鬼》和《钢琴课》这三部翻拍作品中对“象征性”意象的拙劣处理，便是其中最明目张胆的例子。我想到两个可能的原因是：第一，为了迎合那些自诩为知识分子的精英观众，让他们以一种安全、冷静的距离观看电影，同时为映后咖啡馆里的影评仪式收集素材。第二，为了影响甚至控制影评人及其评论。这种夸张的象征主义不需要任何天才，只需要对荣格和德里达的误读所激发出的自负。这是一种贬低和腐蚀艺术的虚荣。

Some argue that the film’s Image System is the director’s work and that he or she alone should create it. And I’ve no argument with that, for ultimately the director is responsible for every square inch of every shot in the film. Except… how many working directors understand what I’ve explained above? Few. Perhaps two dozen in the world today. Just the very best, while, unfortunately, the vast majority cannot tell the difference between decorative and expressive photography.

有人认为，电影的影像系统是导演的作品，应该由导演一人创作。对此我并无异议，因为归根结底，导演要对电影中每一个镜头的每一寸画面负责。然而……有多少在职导演真正理解我上面解释的内容呢？寥寥无几。或许当今世界只有二三十位。只有最顶尖的导演才能做到，而遗憾的是，绝大多数导演根本分不清装饰性摄影和表现性摄影的区别。

I argue that the screenwriter should begin the film’s Image System and the director and designers finish it. It’s the writer who first envisions the ground of all imagery, the story’s physical and social world. Often, as we write, we discover that spontaneously we’ve already begun the work, that a pattern of imagery has found its way into our descriptions and dialogue. As we become aware of that, we devise variations and quietly embroider them into the story. If an Image System doesn’t arrive on its own, we invent one. The audience won’t care how we do it; it only wants the story to work.

我认为，电影的意象系统应该由编剧来构建，导演和设计师来完善。编剧首先构想所有意象的基础，即故事的物质和社会世界。通常，在写作过程中，我们会发现，我们已经自发地开始了这项工作，某种意象模式已经融入到我们的描述和对话中。当我们意识到这一点时，我们会构思出各种变体，并悄然地将它们融入故事中。如果意象系统没有自然而然地出现，我们就创造一个。观众不会在意我们是如何做到的；他们只希望故事能够成功。

TITLES

标题

A film’s title is the marketing centerpiece that “positions” the audience, preparing it for the experience ahead. Screenwriters, therefore, cannot indulge in literary, nontitle titles: TESTAMENT, for example, is actually a film about postnuclear holocaust; LOOKS AND SMILES portrays desolate lives on welfare. My favorite nontitle tile is MOMENT BY MOMENT. MOMENT BY MOMENT is the working title I always use until I figure out the title.

电影的片名是营销的核心，它能“定位”观众，让他们为即将观看的影片做好准备。因此，编剧不能使用文学性强、非标题式的片名：例如，《遗嘱》（TESTAMENT）实际上是一部关于核战后浩劫的电影；《微笑与微笑》（LOOKS AND SMILES）描绘的是靠救济金度日的凄凉生活。我最喜欢的非标题式片名是《分分秒秒》（MOMENT BY MOMENT）。在最终确定片名之前，《分分秒秒》一直是我的工作片名。

To title means to name. An effective title points to something solid that is actually in the story—character, setting, theme, or genre. The best titles often name two or all elements at once.

标题意味着命名。一个好的标题应该指向故事中实际存在的某些要素——人物、场景、主题或类型。优秀的标题往往能同时涵盖两个或所有要素。

JAWS names a character, sets the story in the wilds, and gives us the theme, man against nature, in the Action/Adventure genre. KRAMER VS. KRAMER names two characters, a divorce theme, and Domestic Drama. STAR WARS titles an epic conflict of galactic warriors. PERSONA suggests a cast of psychologically troubled characters and a theme of hidden identities. LA DOLCE VITA places us in a decadent setting among the urban rich. MY BEST FRIEND’S WEDDING establishes characters, setting, and Romantic Comedy.

《大白鲨》片名点明了人物，故事背景设定在荒野，主题是人与自然的对抗，属于动作/冒险类型。《克莱默夫妇》片名点明了两个人物，主题是离婚，属于家庭伦理剧。《星球大战》片名展现了一场星际战士之间的史诗级冲突。《假面》暗示了一群心理受创的角色以及隐藏身份的主题。《甜蜜的生活》将我们带入都市富豪们纸醉金迷的生活。《我最好朋友的婚礼》则设定了人物、场景和浪漫喜剧的元素。

A title, of course, isn’t the only marketing consideration. As the legendary Harry Cohn once observed, “MOGAMBO is a terrible title. MOGAMBO, starring Clark Gable and Ava Gardner, is a great f… ing title.”

当然，片名并非唯一的营销考量因素。正如传奇影评人哈里·科恩曾经说过的那样，“《莫甘博》这个片名糟透了。但由克拉克·盖博和艾娃·加德纳主演的《莫甘博》却是个绝妙的片名。”

#↩

19
19
A WRITER’S METHOD
一位作家的方法

Professional writers may or may not receive critical acclaim, but they’re in control of the craft, have access to their talent, improve their performance over the years, and make a living from the art. A struggling writer may at times produce quality, but from day to day he cannot make his talent perform when and as he wants, doesn’t progress in quality from story to story, and receives little, if any, income from his efforts. On the whole, the difference between those who succeed and those who struggle is their opposed methods of work: inside out versus outside in.

专业作家或许能获得评论界的赞誉，或许不能，但他们掌控着创作，能够充分发挥自己的才能，不断提升写作水平，并以此谋生。而苦苦挣扎的作家或许偶尔也能写出佳作，但他们无法随心所欲地发挥才能，作品质量也难以提升，最终几乎得不到任何收入。总而言之，成功者和苦苦挣扎者的区别在于他们截然不同的创作方式：一种是“由内而外”的创作模式，另一种则是“由外而内”的创作模式。

WRITING FROM THE OUTSIDE IN

从外部视角向内写作

The struggling writer tends to have a way of working that goes something like this: He dreams up an idea, noodles on it for a while, then rushes straight to the keyboard:

写作遇到瓶颈的人往往有这样一种工作方式：他先构思出一个想法，琢磨一会儿，然后直接冲到键盘前开始写作：

EXT. HOUSE—DAY

外景：房屋—日

Description, description, description. Characters A and B enter.

描述，描述，描述。角色A和B出场。

CHARACTER A

角色A

Dialogue, dialogue, dialogue.

对话，对话，对话。

CHARACTER B

角色 B

Dialogue, dialogue, dialogue.

对话，对话，对话。

Description, description, description, description, description.

描述，描述，描述，描述，描述。

He imagines and writes, writes and dreams until he reaches page 120 and stops. Then he hands out Xerox copies to friends and back come their reactions: “Oh, it’s nice, and I love that scene in the garage when they threw paint all over each other, was that funny or what? And when the little kid came down at night in his pajamas, how sweet! The scene on the beach was so romantic, and when the car blew up, exciting. But I don’t know… there’s something about the ending… and the middle… and the way it starts… that just doesn’t work for me.”

他构思、写作，写作、做梦，直到写到120页才停笔。然后他把复印件分发给朋友们，朋友们纷纷反馈：“哦，写得不错，我喜欢他们在车库里互相泼油漆的那段，是不是很搞笑？还有那个小男孩晚上穿着睡衣下来，真可爱！海滩上的那段太浪漫了，汽车爆炸那段也刺激极了。但是，我不知道……结尾……还有中间部分……以及开头……总感觉哪里不对劲。”

So the struggling writer gathers friends’ reactions and his own thoughts to start the second draft with this strategy: “How can I keep the six scenes that I love and that everyone else loves and somehow pretzel this film through them in a way that’ll work?” With a little more thought he’s back at the keyboard:

于是，这位苦苦挣扎的编剧收集了朋友们的反馈和自己的想法，开始着手第二稿，并采取了这样的策略：“我该如何保留我和大家都喜欢的那六个场景，并巧妙地将它们融入到整部电影中，使其行之有效？” 经过一番思考，他又回到了键盘前：

INT. HOUSE—NIGHT

内景，房屋—夜晚

Description, description, description. Characters A and C enter while Character B watches from hiding.

描述，描述，描述。角色A和C出场，角色B则躲在一旁观看。

CHARACTER A

角色A

Dialogue, dialogue, dialogue.

对话，对话，对话。

CHARACTER C

角色C

Dialogue, dialogue, dialogue.

对话，对话，对话。

Description, description, description, description, description.

描述，描述，描述，描述，描述。

He imagines and writes, writes and dreams, but all the while he clings like a drowning man to his favorite scenes until a rewrite comes out the other end. He makes copies and hands them out to friends and back come reactions: “It’s different, decidedly different. But I’m so glad you kept that scene in the garage and with the kid in his pajamas and the car on the beach… great scenes. But… there’s still something about that ending and the middle and the way it starts that just doesn’t work for me.”

他构思、写作，写作、梦想，但始终像溺水者般紧紧抓住自己最喜欢的场景，直到最终的修改稿诞生。他复印几份，分发给朋友，朋友们的反馈纷至沓来：“不一样了，确实不一样。但我很高兴你保留了车库里的那场戏，还有孩子穿着睡衣，车子停在沙滩上的那场戏……很棒的场景。但是……结尾、中间部分以及开头，总感觉哪里不对劲。”

The writer then does a third draft and a fourth and a fifth but the process is always the same: He clings to his favorite scenes, twisting a new telling through them in hopes of finding a story that works. Finally a year’s gone by and he’s burned out. He declares the screenplay perfect and hands it to his agent, who reads it without enthusiasm, but because he’s an agent, he does what he must. He too makes copies, papers Hollywood, and back come reader reports: “Very nicely written, good crisp, actable dialogue, vivid scene description, fine attention to detail, the story sucks. PASS ON IT.” The writer blames the Philistine tastes of Hollywood and gears up for his next project.

编剧接着写了第三稿、第四稿、第五稿，但过程始终如一：他紧紧抓住自己最喜欢的几个场景，反复琢磨，试图从中找到一个合适的故事。一年过去了，他终于精疲力竭。他宣称剧本完美无缺，交给经纪人。经纪人读完后兴致索然，但毕竟是经纪人，他只能照办。他也复印了几份，寄往好莱坞，然后收到了读者的反馈：“文笔优美，对话简洁明快，场景描写生动，细节处理到位，但故事烂透了。别投稿。” 编剧把责任归咎于好莱坞的庸俗品味，然后开始着手下一个项目。

WRITING FROM THE INSIDE OUT

由内而外地写作

Successful writers tend to use the reverse process. If, hypothetically and optimistically, a screenplay can be written from first idea to last draft in six months, these writers typically spend the first four of those six months writing on stacks of three-by-five cards: a stack for each act—three, four, perhaps more. On these cards they create the story’s step-outline.

成功的编剧往往采用相反的方法。假设（乐观地）一个剧本从最初构思到最终定稿可以在六个月内完成，这些编剧通常会在这六个月的前四个月里，用一叠叠三乘五英寸的卡片进行创作：每一叠卡片对应一个场景——三幕、四幕，甚至更多。他们在这些卡片上勾勒出故事的框架。

Step-Outline

步骤概要

As the term implies, a step-outline is the story told in steps.

顾名思义，分步大纲就是分步骤讲述故事。

Using one- or two-sentence statements, the writer simply and clearly describes what happens in each scene, how it builds and turns. For example: “He enters expecting to find her at home, but instead discovers her note saying she’s left for good.”

作者运用一两句话，简洁明了地描述了每个场景中发生的事情，以及情节是如何发展和转变的。例如：“他进门本以为会见到她，却发现她留了一张字条，说她永远离开了。”

On the back of each card the writer indicates what step in the design of the story he sees this scene fulfilling—at least for the moment. Which scenes set up the Inciting Incident? Which is the Inciting Incident? First Act Climax? Perhaps a Mid-Act Climax? Second Act? Third? Fourth? Or more? He does this for Central Plot and subplots alike.

在每张卡片的背面，作者都会标明他认为该场景在故事设计中扮演着怎样的角色——至少目前如此。哪些场景为引子事件做了铺垫？哪个场景本身就是引子事件？是第一幕的高潮？还是中幕的高潮？第二幕？第三幕？第四幕？或者更多？他对主线剧情和支线剧情都做了这样的标注。

He confines himself to a few stacks of cards for months on end for this critical reason: He wants to destroy his work. Taste and experience tell him that 90 percent of everything he writes, regardless of his genius, is mediocre at best. In his patient search for quality, he must create far more material than he can use, then destroy it. He may sketch a scene a dozen different ways before finally throwing the idea of the scene out of the outline. He may destroy sequences, whole acts. A writer secure in his talent knows there’s no limit to what he can create, and so he trashes everything less than his best on a quest for a gem-quality story.

他连续几个月都把自己封闭在几叠卡片中，原因只有一个：他想毁掉自己的作品。品味和经验告诉他，无论他多么才华横溢，他写的东西90%充其量也只是平庸之作。为了耐心地追求卓越，他必须创作远超实际所需的素材，然后再将其销毁。他可能会用十几种不同的方式勾勒同一个场景，最终才将这个场景从大纲中剔除。他可能会销毁某些段落，甚至整幕。一个对自己才华充满自信的作家深知自己的创作潜力无限，因此，为了追求完美，他会毫不犹豫地舍弃所有不够优秀的作品。

This process, however, doesn’t mean the writer isn’t filling pages. Day after day a huge stack grows on the side of the desk: but these are biographies, the fictional world and its history, thematic notations, images, even snippets of vocabulary and idiom. Research and imaginings of all kinds fill a file cabinet while the story is disciplined to the step-outline.

然而，这并不意味着作者没有在创作。日复一日，桌边堆积着厚厚一摞稿件：但这些都是人物传记、虚构世界及其历史、主题笔记、图片，甚至还有词汇和习语片段。各种各样的研究和想象都塞满了文件柜，而故事则严格按照分步大纲进行。

Finally, after weeks or months, the writer discovers his Story Climax. With that in hand, he reworks, as needed, backward from it. At last he has a story. Now he goes to friends, but not asking for a day out of their lives—which is what we ask when we want a conscientious person to read a screenplay. Instead he pours a cup of coffee and asks for ten minutes. Then he pitches his story.

最终，经过数周或数月的酝酿，作者找到了故事的高潮。有了它，他便开始根据需要，从高潮倒推进行修改。最终，他得到了一个完整的故事。现在，他去找朋友们，但不会像我们想找个认真负责的人读剧本时那样，请求他们抽出一天的时间。相反，他会倒上一杯咖啡，请求十分钟的时间。然后，他便开始讲述他的故事。

The writer never shows his step-outline to people because it’s a tool, too cryptic for anyone but the writer to follow. Instead, at this critical stage, he wants to tell or pitch his story so he can see it unfold in time, watch it play on the thoughts and feelings of another human being. He wants to look in that person’s eyes and see the story happen there. So he pitches and studies the reactions: Is my friend hooked by my Inciting Incident? Listening and leaning in? Or are his eyes wandering? Am I holding him as I build and turn the progressions? And when I hit the Climax, do I get a strong reaction of the kind I want?

作者从不向人展示他的故事大纲，因为它只是一种工具，除了作者自己，其他人根本无法理解。相反，在这个关键阶段，他想亲自讲述或推介他的故事，以便观察故事如何随着时间的推移而展开，感受它如何影响另一个人的思想和情感。他想注视着听众的眼睛，亲眼见证故事的发生。因此，他会进行推介，并观察听众的反应：我的朋友是否被我的开场白所吸引？他是否认真聆听并投入其中？还是他的目光游离？在构建和推进情节的过程中，我是否牢牢抓住了他的注意力？当故事达到高潮时，我是否得到了我所期望的那种强烈反应？

Any story pitched from its step-outline to an intelligent, sensitive person must be able to grab attention, hold interest for ten minutes, and pay it off by moving him to a meaningful, emotional experience—just as my LES DIABOLIQUE pitch hooked, held, and moved you. Regardless of genre, if a story can’t work in ten minutes, how will it work in 110 minutes? It won’t get better when it gets bigger. Everything that’s wrong with it in a ten-minute pitch is ten times worse onscreen.

任何故事，只要从大纲开始，向一位有智慧、有同理心的人推介，都必须能够抓住他的注意力，让他保持兴趣十分钟，并最终让他获得深刻的情感体验——就像我当初推介《恶魔》时那样，既吸引了你，又让你保持兴趣，最终感动了你。无论什么类型，如果一个故事在十分钟内都行不通，那么它在110分钟内又如何能行得通呢？故事不会因为时长增加而变得更好。十分钟推介中存在的所有问题，在银幕上都会放大十倍。

Until a good majority of listeners respond with enthusiasm, there’s no point going forward. “With enthusiasm” doesn’t mean people leap up and kiss you on both cheeks, rather they whisper “Wow” and fall silent. A fine work of art—music, dance, painting, story—has the power to silence the chatter in the mind and lift us to another place. When a story, pitched from a step-outline, is so strong it brings silence—no comments, no criticism, just a look of pleasure—that’s a hell of a thing and time is too precious to waste on a story that hasn’t that power. Now the writer’s ready to move to the next stage—the treatment.

除非绝大多数听众都表现出热情，否则继续下去毫无意义。“热情”并非指人们会跳起来亲吻你的双颊，而是他们会轻声惊叹“哇”，然后安静下来。优秀的艺术作品——音乐、舞蹈、绘画、故事——拥有让思绪平静下来，并将我们带入另一个境界的力量。当一个根据大纲构思的故事如此精彩，以至于能让听众鸦雀无声——没有评论，没有批评，只有愉悦的表情——那真是太棒了，时间如此宝贵，不应该浪费在一个没有这种力量的故事上。现在，作者可以进入下一个阶段——剧本大纲。

Treatment

治疗

To “treat” the step-outline, the writer expands each scene from its one or two sentences to a paragraph or more of double-spaced, present-tense, moment by moment description:

为了“处理”分步大纲，作者将每个场景从一两句话扩展成一段或多段双倍行距、现在时态、逐帧描述的文字：

Dining Room—Day Jack walks in and tosses his briefcase on the chair next to the door. He looks around. The room is empty. He calls her name. Gets no answer. He calls it again, louder and louder. Still no answer. As he pads to the kitchen, he sees a note on the table. Picks it up, reads it. The note says that she has left him for good. He drops in the chair, head in hands, and starts to cry.

餐厅——白天，杰克走进餐厅，把公文包扔到门口的椅子上。他环顾四周，房间里空无一人。他喊她的名字，无人应答。他又喊了一遍，声音越来越大，仍然没有回应。他轻手轻脚地走向厨房，看到桌上有一张纸条。他拿起纸条，读了起来。纸条上说她永远地离开了他。他瘫坐在椅子上，双手抱头，开始哭泣。

In treatment the writer indicates what characters talk about—“he wants her to do this, but she refuses,” for example—but never writes dialogue. Instead, he creates the subtext—the true thoughts and feelings underneath what is said and done. We may think we know what our characters are thinking and feeling, but we don’t know we know until we write it down:

在剧本大纲中，作者会指出人物谈论的内容——例如，“他想让她做这件事，但她拒绝了”——但从不直接写对话。相反，他创造的是潜台词——隐藏在言行背后的真实想法和感受。我们或许认为自己了解人物的所思所想，但只有写下来，我们才能真正确定自己了解。

Dining Room—Day The door opens and Jack leans on the jamb, exhausted from a day of failed and frustrating work. He looks around the room, sees she’s not around, and hopes like hell she’s out. He really doesn’t want to have to deal with her today. To be sure he has the house to himself, he calls her name. Gets no answer. Calls out louder and louder. Still no answer. Good. He’s finally alone. He lifts his briefcase high in the air drops it with a thud onto her precious Chippendale chair next to the door. She hates him for scratching her antiques but today he doesn’t give a damn.

餐厅——白天 门开了，杰克靠在门框上，一天的工作让他筋疲力尽，既失败又令人沮丧。他环顾四周，发现她不在，心里暗暗祈祷她真的出去了。他今天真的不想跟她打交道。为了确定家里只有他一个人，他喊了一声她的名字。没人回应。他越喊越大声。还是没人回应。很好。他终于可以独处了。他高高举起公文包，砰的一声扔到她放在门边那把珍贵的奇彭代尔椅上。她恨他刮花她的古董，但今天他毫不在乎。

Hungry, he heads for the kitchen, but as he crosses the room he notices a note on the dining-room table. It’s one of those damn, annoying notes that she’s always leaving around, taped to the bathroom mirror or the refrigerator or whatever. Irritated, he picks it up and tears it open. Reading it, he discovers that she’s left him for good. As his legs go weak, he drops into a chair, a knot twisting in his gut. His head falls into his hands and he starts to cry. He’s surprised by his outburst, pleased he can still feel some emotion. But his tears are not grief; they’re the dam breaking with relief that the relationship is finally over.

他饥肠辘辘，走向厨房，但穿过房间时，他注意到餐桌上有一张纸条。又是那种该死的、烦人的纸条，她总是到处乱贴，浴室镜子上、冰箱上，或者任何地方。他恼火地拿起纸条，撕开。读完后，他发现她彻底离开了他。他双腿一软，跌坐在椅子上，胃里像打了个结。他双手抱头，开始哭泣。他对自己突然爆发感到惊讶，同时也庆幸自己还能感受到一些情感。但他的眼泪并非悲伤，而是如释重负的泪水，因为这段感情终于结束了。

*  *  *

The forty to sixty scenes of a typical screenplay, treated to a moment by moment description of all action, underlaid with a full subtext of the conscious and unconscious thoughts and feelings of all characters, will produce sixty, eight, ninety, or more double-spaced pages. In the studio system from the 1930s to the 1950s when producers ordered treatments from writers, they were often two hundred to three hundred pages long. The strategy of studio writers was to extract the screenplay from a much larger work so nothing would be overlooked or unthought.

一部典型的电影剧本通常包含四十到六十个场景，如果对所有动作进行逐帧描述，并辅以所有角色意识和潜意识中丰富的思想和情感，最终会形成六十页、八页、九十页甚至更多双倍行距的篇幅。在20世纪30年代到50年代的制片厂制度下，制片人要求编剧撰写剧本大纲时，大纲往往长达两三百页。制片厂编剧的策略是将剧本从一个更大的作品中提炼出来，以确保没有任何遗漏或疏忽之处。

The ten- or twelve-page “treatments” that pass around show business today are not treatments but outlines given enough words that a reader can follow the story. A ten-page outline is not nearly enough material for a screenplay. Today’s writers may not return to the vast treatments of the studio system, but when a step-outline is expanded to a treatment of sixty to ninety pages, creative achievement expands correspondingly.

如今在演艺圈流传的那些十页或十二页的“剧本大纲”并非真正的剧本大纲，而只是用足够的篇幅概括故事梗概，让读者能够理解剧情。十页的大纲远远不足以支撑一个完整的剧本。如今的编剧或许不会再像过去那样撰写篇幅巨大的剧本大纲，但当一个简略的大纲扩展成六十到九十页的剧本大纲时，创作成果也会相应提升。

At the treatment stage, we inevitably discover that things we thought would work a certain way in the step-outline now want to change. Research and imagination never stop, and so the characters and their world are still growing and evolving, leading us to revise any number of scenes. We won’t change the overall design of the story because it worked every time we pitched it. But within that structure scenes may need to be cut, added, or reordered. We rework the treatment until every moment lives vividly, in text and subtext. That done, then and only then does the writer move to the screenplay itself.

在剧本大纲阶段，我们不可避免地会发现，原本在分步大纲中设想的某些情节现在需要修改。研究和想象永无止境，因此人物及其世界也在不断发展演变，这促使我们修改许多场景。我们不会因为故事的整体架构每次都能成功就改变它。但在架构之内，场景可能需要删减、添加或重新排序。我们会反复修改剧本大纲，直到每个瞬间都鲜活生动，字里行间都充满张力。只有到了这一步，编剧才能真正开始撰写剧本。

SCREENPLAY

剧本

Writing a screenplay from a thorough treatment is a joy and often runs at a clip of five to ten pages per day. We now convert treatment description to screen description and add dialogue. And dialogue written at this point is invariably the finest dialogue we’ve ever written. Our characters have had tape over their mouths for so long, they can’t wait to talk, and unlike so many films in which all characters speak with the same vocabulary and style, dialogue written after in-depth preparation creates character-specific voices. They don’t all sound like one another and they don’t all sound like the writer.

根据详尽的剧本大纲撰写剧本是一件乐事，通常一天就能写出五到十页。接下来，我们将大纲描述转化为剧本描述，并添加对白。而此时写出的对白，往往是我们写过的最精彩的对白。我们的角色们仿佛被胶带封住了嘴巴，迫不及待地想要开口说话。与许多电影中所有角色都使用相同词汇和风格的对话不同，经过深入准备后创作的对白，能够塑造出角色独特的声音。他们彼此之间不会雷同，也不会都带有编剧的个人风格。

At the first draft stage, changes and revisions will still be needed. When characters are allowed to speak, scenes in treatment you thought would work a certain way now want to alter direction. When you find such a fault, it can rarely be fixed with a simple rewrite of dialogue or behavior. Rather, you must go back into the treatment and rework the setups, then perhaps go beyond the faulty scene to redo the payoff. A number of polishes may be necessary until you reach the final draft. You must develop your judgment and taste, a nose for your own bad writing, then call upon a relentless courage to root out weaknesses and turn them into strengths.

初稿阶段仍然需要修改和润色。当角色开始说话后，你原本设想的场景走向可能会发生变化。当你发现这类问题时，仅仅重写对话或行为是很难解决的。你必须回到剧本大纲，重新调整场景设置，甚至可能需要深入到问题场景之外，重新构思结尾。在最终定稿之前，可能需要反复润色。你必须培养自己的判断力和鉴赏力，敏锐地察觉自己写作中的不足，然后鼓起勇气，不遗余力地找出弱点，并将其转化为优势。

If you shortcut the process and rush straight to screenplay from outline, the truth is that your first draft is not a screenplay, it’s a surrogate treatment—a narrow, unexplored, unimprovised, tissue-thin treatment. Event choice and story design must be given free rein to consume your imagination and knowledge. Turning Points must be imagined, discarded, and reimagined, then played out in text and subtext. Otherwise you have little hope of achieving excellence. Now, how and when do you want to do that? In treatment or screenplay? Either may work, but, more often than not, screenplay is a trap. The wise writer puts off the writing of dialogue for as long as possible because the premature writing of dialogue chokes creativity.

如果你走捷径，直接从大纲跳到剧本，那么你的初稿实际上并不是剧本，而只是一个近似的剧本大纲——一个狭隘、未经探索、缺乏即兴发挥、单薄的大纲。事件的选择和故事的设计必须充分发挥你的想象力和知识。转折点必须反复构思、推翻、再重新构思，最终在文本和潜台词中呈现出来。否则，你很难达到卓越的水平。那么，你想如何以及何时做到这一点呢？是在大纲阶段还是剧本阶段？两者都可行，但通常情况下，剧本阶段是一个陷阱。明智的编剧会尽可能推迟对话的创作，因为过早地撰写对话会扼杀创造力。

Writing from the outside in—writing dialogue in search of scenes, writing scenes in search of story— is the least creative method. Screenwriters habitually overvalue dialogue because they’re the only words we write that actually reach the audience. All else is assumed by the film’s images. If we type out dialogue before we know what happens , we inevitably fall in love with our words; we’re loath to play with and explore events, to discover how fascinating our characters might become, because it would mean cutting our priceless dialogue. All improvisation ceases and our so-called rewriting is tinkering with speeches.

从外而内进行创作——先写对话寻找场景，再写场景寻找故事——是最缺乏创造力的方法。编剧们往往过分重视对话，因为对话是我们写出的唯一真正能传达给观众的文字。其他一切都由电影画面来呈现。如果我们事先不知道剧情走向就写出对话，我们必然会爱上这些文字；我们不愿去探索和尝试，不愿去发现角色可能变得多么引人入胜，因为这意味着要删掉那些宝贵的对话。所有的即兴发挥都戛然而止，我们所谓的修改变成了对台词的修修补补。

What’s more, the premature writing of dialogue is the slowest way to work. It may send you in circles for years before you finally realize that not all your children are going to walk and talk their way to the screen; not every idea is worth being a motion picture. When do you want to find that out? Two years from now or two months from now? If you write the dialogue first, you’ll be blind to this truth and wander forever. If you write from the inside out, you’ll realize in the outline stage that you can’t get the story to work. Nobody likes it when pitched. In truth, you don’t like it. So you toss it in the drawer. Maybe years from now you’ll pick it up and solve it, but for now you go on to your next idea.

更重要的是，过早地写对话是最慢的创作方式。它可能会让你兜圈子好几年，最终才意识到并非所有想法都能搬上银幕；并非每个创意都值得拍成电影。你想什么时候知道答案？两年后还是两个月后？如果你先写对话，就会对这个真相视而不见，永远迷失方向。如果你从内而外地写作，在构思阶段就会发现故事行不通。没人喜欢这样的剧本。说实话，你自己也不喜欢。于是你把它扔进抽屉。也许几年后你会重新拾起它，找到解决办法，但现在你只能继续构思下一个想法。

As I offer this method to you, I’m fully aware that each of us, by trial and error, must find our own method, that indeed some writers short-cut the treatment stage and produce quality screenplays, and that in fact a few have written very well from the outside in. But I’m also left to wonder what brilliance they might have achieved had they taken greater pains. For the inside-out method is a way of working that’s both disciplined and free, designed to encourage your finest work.

我向你介绍这种方法时，完全明白每个人都必须通过反复尝试才能找到适合自己的方法；的确，有些编剧会省略剧本构思阶段，直接创作出高质量的剧本；也确实有一些编剧是从外向内写出非常优秀的作品。但我也不禁会想，如果他们当初能更用心一些，又能创作出怎样的佳作呢？因为这种由内而外的创作方法既严谨又自由，旨在激发你创作出最优秀的作品。

#↩

FADE OUT

淡出

You have pursued Story to its final chapter, and, with this step, taken your career in a direction many writers fear. Some, dreading that awareness of how they do what they do would cripple their spontaneity, never study the craft. Instead, they march along in a lockstep of unconscious habit, thinking it’s instinct. Their dreams of creating unique works of power and wonder are seldom, if ever, realized. They put in long, tough days, for no matter how it’s taken, the writer’s road is never smooth, and because they have a gift, from time to time their efforts draw applause, but in their secret selves they know they’re just taking talent for a walk. Such writers remind me of the protagonist of a fable my father loved to recite:

你已经将故事追寻到了最终篇章，而这一步也让你的职业生涯走向了许多作家所畏惧的方向。有些人害怕意识到自己创作的方式会扼杀他们的灵感，因此从未深入学习写作技巧。相反，他们只是机械地遵循着无意识的习惯，以为那是本能。他们创作出独一无二、充满力量和奇迹的作品的梦想，即使有，也鲜少实现。他们日复一日地辛勤工作，因为无论如何，写作之路从来都不是一帆风顺的。尽管他们拥有天赋，他们的努力偶尔会赢得掌声，但在他们内心深处，他们知道自己只是在挥霍天赋而已。这样的作家让我想起了我父亲喜欢讲述的一个寓言故事的主人公：

High above the forest floor, a millipede strolled along the branch of a tree, her thousand pairs of legs swinging in an easy gait. From the tree top, song birds looked down, fascinated by the synchronization of the millipede’s stride. “That’s an amazing talent,” chirped the songbirds. “You have more limbs than we can count. How do you do it?” And for the first time in her life the millipede thought about this. “Yes,” she wondered, “how do I do what I do?” As she turned to look back, her bristling legs suddenly ran into one another and tangled like vines of ivy. The songbirds laughed as the millipede, in a panic of confusion, twisted herself into a knot and fell to the earth below.

在高高的森林之上，一只千足虫沿着树枝缓缓踱步，上千对腿轻松地摆动着。树梢上的鸣禽俯视着，被千足虫步伐的协调性深深吸引。“真是惊人的天赋！”鸣禽们叽叽喳喳地说，“你的腿多得我们都数不过来。你是怎么做到的？”千足虫生平第一次思考这个问题。“是啊，”她疑惑道，“我是怎么做到的？”正当她转头回头看时，她那长满刚毛的腿突然纠缠在一起，像藤蔓一样缠绕在一起。鸣禽们哄堂大笑，只见千足虫惊慌失措，把自己扭成一个结，摔落到下面的地面上。

You too may sense this panic. I know that when confronted with a rush of insights even the most experienced writer can be knocked off stride. Fortunately, my father’s fable had an Act Two:

你或许也能感受到这种恐慌。我知道，即使是最有经验的作家，在灵感如潮水般涌来时，也会被打乱节奏。幸运的是，我父亲的寓言故事还有第二幕：

On the forest floor, the millipede, realizing that only her pride was hurt, slowly, carefully, limb by limb, unraveled herself. With patience and hard work, she studied and flexed and tested her appendages, until she was able to stand and walk. What was once instinct became knowledge. She realized she didn’t have to move at her old, slow, rote pace. She could amble, strut, prance, even run and jump. Then, as never before, she listened to the symphony of the songbirds and let music touch her heart. Now in perfect command of thousands of talented legs, she gathered courage and, with a style of her own, danced and danced a dazzling dance that astonished all the creatures of her world.

在森林的地面上，千足虫意识到自己只是自尊心受到了伤害，便小心翼翼地，一节一节地舒展开身体。她耐心而努力地研究、伸展、测试自己的肢体，直到能够站立行走。曾经的本能变成了知识。她意识到自己不必再像以前那样缓慢而机械地移动。她可以漫步、昂首阔步、轻快地跳跃，甚至可以奔跑和跳跃。然后，她前所未有地聆听着鸟儿的交响乐，让音乐触动她的心弦。如今，她完美地掌控着成千上万条灵巧的腿，鼓起勇气，跳起了独具特色的舞步，翩翩起舞，令人叹为观止，让世间万物都为之惊叹。

Write every day, line by line, page by page, hour by hour. Keep Story at hand. Use what you learn from it as a guide, until command of its principles becomes as natural as the talent you were born with. Do this despite fear. For above all else, beyond imagination and skill, what the world asks of you is courage, courage to risk rejection, ridicule and failure. As you follow the quest for stories told with meaning and beauty, study thoughtfully but write boldly. Then, like the hero of the fable, your dance will dazzle the world.

每天写作，一行一行，一页一页，一小时一小时。让《故事》触手可及。以你从中学到的东西为指引，直到你对它的理解如同与生俱来的天赋般自然流畅。即使恐惧也要坚持下去。因为最重要的是，超越想象力和技巧，世界需要你的是勇气，是敢于承担被拒绝、被嘲笑和失败的风险的勇气。当你追寻那些充满意义和美感的故事时，要深思熟虑地学习，但也要大胆地写作。然后，就像寓言中的英雄一样，你的舞步将惊艳世界。

SUGGESTED READINGS

推荐阅读

My education owes a debt to the writers of many hundreds of books and essays on the art of story. Below, however, is a shortlist of works that have been the most insightful, the most inspiring.

我的教育得益于数百本关于故事艺术的书籍和文章的作者们。以下列出的是其中最具洞察力、最鼓舞人心的作品。

Aristotle’s Poetics. Translation and commentary by Stephen Halliwell. Chapel Hill: University of North Carolina Press, 1986.

亚里士多德《诗学》。斯蒂芬·哈利韦尔译注。教堂山：北卡罗来纳大学出版社，1986年。

Bjorkman, Stig, Torsten Manns, and Jonas Sima. Bergman on Bergman. Translation by Paul Britten Austin. New York: Simon & Schuster, 1973.

比约克曼、斯蒂格、托斯滕·曼斯和乔纳斯·西玛。《伯格曼论伯格曼》。保罗·布里顿·奥斯汀译。纽约：西蒙与舒斯特出版社，1973年。

Booth, Wayne C. The Rhetoric of Fiction. 2d ed. Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1983.

Booth, Wayne C.《小说的修辞学》。第2版。芝加哥：芝加哥大学出版社，1983年。

Burke, Kenneth. The Philosophy of Literary Form. Berkeley: University of California Press, 1974.

伯克，肯尼斯。《文学形式的哲学》。伯克利：加州大学出版社，1974年。

Burnett, Hallie, and Whit Burnett. The Fiction Writer’s Handbook. New York: Barnes & Noble, 1979.

伯内特，哈莉和惠特·伯内特。《小说家手册》。纽约：巴诺书店，1979年。

Campbell, Joseph. The Hero with a Thousand Faces. 2d ed. Princeton, N.J.: Princeton University Press, 1972.

坎贝尔，约瑟夫。《千面英雄》。第2版。普林斯顿，新泽西州：普林斯顿大学出版社，1972年。

Friedman, Norman. Form and Meaning in Fiction. Athens: University of Georgia Press, 1975.

弗里德曼，诺曼。《小说的形式与意义》。雅典：佐治亚大学出版社，1975年。

Gardner, John. On Becoming a Novelist. New York: Harper & Row, 1983.

加德纳，约翰。《如何成为一名小说家》。纽约：哈珀与罗出版社，1983年。

James, Henry. The Art of the Novel. Edited by R. P. Blackmur. New York: Scribner’s, 1932.

詹姆斯，亨利。《小说的艺术》。R·P·布莱克默编辑。纽约：斯克里布纳出版社，1932年。

Koestler, Arthur. The Act of Creation. New York: Macmillan, 1964.

科斯特勒，亚瑟。《创造的行为》。纽约：麦克米伦出版社，1964年。

Langer, Susanne K. Feeling and Form. New York: Macmillan, 1977.

Langer, Susanne K. 感觉与形式。纽约：麦克米伦出版社，1977 年。

Lawson, John Howard. Film: The Creative Process. New York: Hill & Wang, 1964.

劳森，约翰·霍华德。《电影：创作过程》。纽约：希尔与王出版社，1964年。

Lawson, John Howard. The Theory and Technique of Playwriting and Screenwriting. New York: G.P. Putnam’s, 1949.

劳森，约翰·霍华德。《戏剧和电影剧本创作的理论与技巧》。纽约：G.P. Putnam’s出版社，1949年。

Mamet, David. On Directing Film. New York: Viking Press, 1981.

马梅特，大卫。《论电影导演》。纽约：维京出版社，1981年。

Rowe, Kenneth T. Write That Play. New York: Funk & Wagnalls, 1939, 1968.

罗威，肯尼斯·T.《写出那部剧本》。纽约：Funk & Wagnalls出版社，1939年，1968年。

Scholes, Robert, and Robert Kellogg. The Nature of Narrative. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1966.

Scholes, Robert 和 Robert Kellogg。《叙事的本质》。牛津：牛津大学出版社，1966 年。

ACKNOWLEDGMENTS

致谢

For her sensitivity to the truth, for her unblinking editorial eye and omnivorous will to omit needless words, her unerring logic, optimism, inspiration … for her love, I thank my wife, Suzanne Childs.

我感谢我的妻子苏珊娜·查尔兹，感谢她对真相的敏锐，感谢她毫不眨眼的编辑眼光和不加修饰的意志，感谢她精准的逻辑、乐观的态度、灵感……感谢她的爱。

As the lucky associate of astute accomplices willing to suffer rough drafts, close holes, sand ragged edges, and wisely point out that things don’t always mean what their author thinks they mean, I thank Jess Money, Gail McNamara, and my editor, Andrew Albanese.

作为有幸与精明的同谋们合作的伙伴，他们愿意忍受粗糙的草稿、填补漏洞、打磨粗糙的边缘，并明智地指出事物并不总是像作者认为的那样有意义，我感谢 Jess Money、Gail McNamara 和我的编辑 Andrew Albanese。

If it weren’t for my agent’s uncanny timing, I would have procrastinated this book into the next century. Thank you, Debra Rodman.

要不是我的经纪人时机把握得太好了，这本书恐怕要拖到下个世纪才能出版了。谢谢你，黛布拉·罗德曼。

If it weren’t for my publisher’s persistence, I would have procrastinated my agent’s promptings into the next century. Thank you, Judith Regan.

若非出版商的坚持不懈，我恐怕会把经纪人的催促拖到下个世纪。谢谢你，朱迪思·里根。

If it weren’t for the support of the Evans Scholars Foundation and the minds I met at the University of Michigan, my life would have been diminished. I offer my gratitude to Kenneth Rowe, John Arthos, Hugh Norton, Claribel Baird, Donald Hall, and all other professors whose names I’ve forgotten, but whose brilliant teachings have braced my days.

若非埃文斯学者基金会的支持以及我在密歇根大学遇到的良师益友，我的人生将会黯然失色。我衷心感谢肯尼斯·罗、约翰·阿索斯、休·诺顿、克拉丽贝尔·贝尔德、唐纳德·霍尔，以及所有其他我已遗忘姓名的教授，他们渊博的学识曾激励着我，照亮我的每一天。

Lastly, most importantly, my students. Over the years my understanding of the art of story has grown thanks, in great part, to the questions you’ve asked, questions both perceptive and practical, that have sent me further and deeper in search of answers. This book would not exist without you.

最后，也是最重要的，我要感谢我的学生们。多年来，我对故事艺术的理解不断加深，这很大程度上要归功于你们提出的问题——那些既富有洞察力又切实可行的问题，它们引领我更深入地探寻答案。没有你们，这本书就不会存在。
